speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Treasury Board; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: OUTLINE BY MINISTER OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to table the Main Estimates for 1988-89, which total $119 billion. These estimates support what my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), said in his recent Budget speech about the fiscal intentions of this Government.
We are firmly committed to restraint through good management of the public's resources while responding with positive actions to introduce new initiatives in high priority areas. These Main Estimates are consistent with the planned expenditure levels outlined in the Budget earlier this month.
Our total spending plan for 1988-89, which includes these Main Estimates and reserves for Supplementary Estimates,
totals $132 billion. That is 5.5 per cent above planned spending in 1987-88. If we exclude public debt charges and look at program expenditures, the growth is only 4.3 per cent.
The average annual increase in budgetary expenditures of 4.9 per cent over the last four years contrasts sharply with the average increases of more than 15 per cent in the preceding five years. Excluding public debt charges, we are looking at an average increase of 3.7 per cent versus 14 per cent in the previous period.
The Main Estimates increase by 7.7 per cent over the comparable 1987-88 level. This growth rate is accommodated within the over-all 5.5 per cent growth in planned budgetary expenditures.
The growth in Main Estimates is larger than that targeted for total spending for the year because the Government has built a greater portion of its new spending initiatives into the Main Estimates than it was able to last year, leaving fewer resources for in-year adjustments through Supplementary Estimates in 1988-89.
These Main Estimates provide for a number of new initiatives that the Government has announced over the past few months to respond to the pressing needs of Canadians. They include $306 million for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, $312 million for the western diversification office, a $197 million increase for other regional development initiatives such as that for northern Ontario, $296 million to complete the $1.1 billion special grains program for the 1987 crop year, and $40 million of the $210 million to be spent on the National Drug Strategy over a five-year period.
The Government has recently announced a number of new initiatives which are not included in these Main Estimates. Further endeavours in the area of science and technology and increased programming for the elderly will appear in Supplementary Estimates over the course of 1988-89.
The Government's child care strategy will be built into estimates following further discussion with provincial governments and the passage of legislation. Funding for all of these is incorporated in the $132 billion expenditure plan within the growth of 4.3 per cent in program expenditures.
Apart from the new initiatives, I would like to outline briefly where the growth in estimates has occurred. Public debt charges are $3.9 billion or 13.7 per cent higher than last year. This burden can be lightened only over the long term through good fiscal management and continued reductions in the level of the deficit.
As well, we are providing an additional one-half billion dollars to the provinces to help finance health, educational and welfare services.
In addition, direct transfer payments to the provincial and territorial governments will rise by almost $1 billion under equalization and other programs.
February 23, 1988

Direct payments to elderly Canadians will rise through an additional $860 million in old age security payments and a further $134 million in Guaranteed Income Supplements.
Thus, of the $8.5 billion increase in these Main Estimates, $3.9 billion or 45 per cent is accounted for by public debt charges and $2.4 billion or 28 per cent relates to increased expenditures for large social programs, including support for health care and education and the direct support to the provinces and territories which I have just mentioned.
The Main Estimates can be divided into two categories: statutory and voted expenditures. The statutory items, totalling $78.5 billion, are programs whose spending is covered by separate legislation. Public debt charges, to which 1 have already referred, account for $32 billion or 40 per cent of that.
The remaining $46.5 billion includes over $20 billion in transfer payments to individual Canadians and more than $20 billion in transfers to provincial governments. Elderly Canadians receive about three-quarters of all the transfer payments to individuals.
Payments to the provinces provide funding for health care, post-secondary education, and welfare assistance and enable provinces to provide their residents with a reasonable level of public services at reasonable comparable levels of taxation.
In addition to those cash payments, the Government provides assistance to the provinces in the form of tax transfers which, in 1988-89, will exceed $9 billion, bringing total financing for health, education, social assistance and other public services to some $30 billion.
The other $41 billion of these Main Estimates, which Parliament will be asked to authorize through the appropriation Bill, reflects a wide variety of expenditures across all departments.
These voted appropriations include $10 billion out of a total Defence spending budget of $11.2 billion, most of the regional development expenditures through the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, the Atlantic Opportunities Agency, the western diversification office, as well as the special grains program and other recent initiatives such as the Drug Strategy-
Over the past four years, voted appropriations have risen on average by less than 3 per cent a year in comparison with an average of almost 13 per cent through the early 1980s. This low rate of growth, maintained over four years, reflects our real achievement in managing government more efficiently and sustaining fiscal restraint. Public spending is firmly under control.
As Hon. Members are aware, the estimates also set out the person-year authorities allocated to departments and agencies. In May, 1985, the Government introduced a plan to reduce the size of the Public Service by 15,000 person-years over a five-year period.
Tabling of Documents
We began in 1986-87 with the reduction of some 5,500 person-years. This was followed by a further 3,100 last year and over 1,900 for 1988-89. While we have downsized the Public Service by more than 10,000 person-years, as of February 12, only 634 of the employees affected had actually been laid off.
Over the remaining two years of the program, the Government will reduce its person-year authorities by about one per cent each year and 1 fully expect that the redeployment efforts which are integral to the workforce adjustment policy will continue to be successful in relocating affected employees.
I want to stress that these Main Estimates reflect this Government's efforts to maintain a balance between spending restraint and the introduction of new initiatives aimed at responding to the needs of the average Canadian.
In accordance with the normal procedures of the House, these estimates will be referred to the appropriate standing committees which will have ample opportunity to review the estimates and report to the House. In June, we will again discuss the estimates in the House before the passage of an appropriation Bill granting full supply.
As my colleague, the Minister of Finance, emphasized, we established a financial plan in 1984, and we have stuck to it, reducing the deficit, controlling expenditures, eliminating waste and duplication, and scaling down the burden of Government.
Within this fiscal framework we have found the necessary resources to meet our policy commitments on regional development, defence, child care, science and technology. We will continue the same prudent course in 1988-89.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: OUTLINE BY MINISTER OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise today to comment on the Treasury Board Estimates and on the Minister's statement, I simply want to say that of all the Estimates that I have seen brought down in this House, none have been brought in to paint over the cracks in the plaster more so than these Estimates today.
We were talking about fiscal responsibility, and the Minister has sat down after making what he thinks are some very constructive comments and which he hopes will wash. The fact of life is that since the Government came to power in September, 1984 the national debt of this country has increased by 66 per cent. Indeed, it has increased by $116.6 billion in 3.5 years.
The Government campaigned in 1984 on fiscal responsibility, and it is still talking in that tone today. For example, in the Government's June White Paper on Tax Reform, it stated in the Estimates that it would only cost $30.1 billion to service the national debt. The Government has since found that it will cost another $2 billion to finance or carry the national debt, because it has not been keeping interest rates under control in

February 23, 1988
Tabling of Documents
the manner in which it has been telling the Canadian public that it has been doing so. The Canadian dollar is increasing in value, but Canadian interest rates are going up.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and members of the Government have bragged in the House about keeping interest rates under control. Today the Canadian public must come up with $2 billion more in interest rates alone simply because the Government has not been able to keep its financial and fiscal responsibility under control. That is a fact of life.
Six months ago the Government announced that it could finance and carry the national debt for this year for $30.1 billion. Today it will cost $32.1 billion, only six months later. The Government talks about keeping interest rates down and it has failed to do so. What I have just mentioned is the proof.
The Premier of Ontario wants to see interest rates kept down. Premier Bourassa, who has been friendly with the Prime Minister in certain cases, wants to keep interest rates down. The Prime Minister is letting down the Premier and the Province of Quebec. The Canadian Chambers of Commerce and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association all want to see the Government keep interest rates down.

They are dismantling it. There is no question about it, it is right here.
Let us talk about all this great work on national defence. I have never seen such a sham in my life. The Government has made a commitment to increase the National Defence budget by 3 per cent annually in real terms. The Government has only done that once in the four years that it has brought down Budgets in this House. Only once out of four years, and in the other three years it did not meet its NATO commitment. Yet here is a Government that talks about doing such great things for national defence.
We heard a lot about the reserves lately, and I want to read a comment here from the Winnipeg Free Press about neglecting the reserves in the Armed Forces. The article states:
When Defence Minister Perrin Beatty introduced his white paper last June, he said, of Canada s reserves: "They have been gravely neglected in recent years. We intend to see these citizens-soldiers, sailors and aviators-receive the recognition they deserve and we will give them a priority that they have not had for several decades."
February 23, 1988

They have certainly been given a priority, Mr. Speaker, because the article further states:
Evidence of this new priority was received by reserve units in Winnipeg this
week. They have been told that in the coming year they will have to get by
with 12.5 per cent less training time than they had this year.
On research and development the Government talks about all the money that it has put out in special programs in research and development. I have figures which show, despite all their rhetoric, that they have actually spent less on research and development than was being spent before.
The Government is not keeping its commitments in that regard. It has downgraded all major research facilities like NRC, NSERC, Science Council, Medical Research Council, agriculture, and forestry. It has downgraded them, cut them by $75 million over the last three years or four years. Then it comes along with a $112.7 million increase and says, "What great people are we".
However, what government Members forgot to mention was that they had cut $60 million from AECL and $70 million from the reserves, which means that they have actually put $93 million less into R and D than they are claiming they did, that they promised to do, and that in fact was there before.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words about the Estimates that are before us and about the possibility, as the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) has said, of spending $132 billion in the next fiscal year. I want to make two major points. They are questions of fairness about how the Government is planning expenditures in 1988-89.
First, Mr. Speaker, I think you would be very interested in Part I of the 1988-89 Estimates, "The Government Expenditure Plan". If we look at the record of what the Conservative Government has been doing, we see that the Government is now spending more money in terms of percentage of its expenditures on the public debt than it was some four years ago. Back in 1984-85 some 20.6 per cent of government expenditures was on interest on the national debt. Some 24.6 per cent of the expenditures of the Government now will be on our national debt. This is an increase of 4 per cent, from 20.6 per cent to 24.6 per cent since the Conservative Party took office in 1984. It is the largest expenditure in any single envelope in the Government of Canada, and it is an increase of some 4 per cent. It is very, very high.
There has been argument in the House about why interest rates in the country should be brought down. If interest rates could be brought down we would save an awful lot of money. If interest rates were to drop by only 1 per cent, the Government of Canada would save $1.4 billion per year. Over four
Tabling of Documents
years, with a drop of 1 per cent, the Government of Canada would save some $9.5 billion.

Mr. Speaker, now that one-quarter of the Government of Canada's expenditures are being used to pay off this country's deficit, to the interest on the deficit, we have now spent about $32 billion of the Estimates for next year.
Mr. Speaker, if the interest rate were to be reduced by 1 per cent, there would be another $4 billion for the Government to spend on Canadians in just one year, and in four years there would be a total of $9.5 billion more.

If the Government would bring down the interest rate, we could use that extra $1.4 billion next year, or the $9.5 billion in four years, for regional development programs.
Second, since the Conservative Party has come to power, the amount of money, in terms of a percentage of the national expenditure, has gone down in regional development. Back in 1984-85, according to the Estimates, some 13.6 per cent of the expenditures of the Canadian Government went to regional development and economic development in Canada. In 198889 it will be down from 13.6 per cent to 10.3 per cent. That is a drop of some 24 per cent in the envelope for economic and regional development, a drop of some 24 per cent. That is not good enough.
If one were to exclude the Special Canadian Grains Program, a program which is very useful in western Canada, for the other regional and economic development programs, the expenditure drop is even greater in terms of a percentage of what the Government spends. It then goes down to some 10 per cent of the national Budget. We are now spending 10 per cent of the national Budget on economic and regional development, compared with 13.6 per cent when the Conservative Party took office some three and a half years ago. It is a drop of 26 per cent in terms of the over-all share which regional development is getting from the Conservative Party across the way.
I make the argument very simply this morning that the Government should be spending a greater share of the expenditures of the people of Canada on economic and regional development.
In the last year some 47 per cent of jobs created in Canada were created in the Province of Ontario. I am very pleased that the Province of Ontario has a lot of job creation, but even in Ontario the vast number of these jobs are located in the area around Toronto. The unemployment rate is high in Windsor. It is high in northern Ontario. There are problems in the City of Hamilton and problems in other areas. Some 47 per cent of the jobs are being created in one province.
What I am arguing today is that we must allocate a greater share of the national expenditure to regional and economic development so that western Canada, the North, parts of

February 23, 1988
Tabling of Documents
Ontario, Quebec, and the Atlantic provinces, share in the economic recovery. Is that too much to ask of the Government across the way?
I repeat the point that when they came to power three and a half years ago, 13.6 per cent of expenditures went to economic and regional development. Now, some three or four years later, they are budgeting for only 10 per cent if we do not include the Special Canadian Grains Program. It is 10.3 per cent, if we include the grains program, for regional and economic development.

Mr. Speaker, federal spending on regional economic development programs has dropped substantially by about 24 per cent, I believe-programs that are vital to Quebec, to western Canada, to the North, to the Atlantic Provinces and to Northern Ontario. This Government is now spending less, percentage wise, then it was spending four years ago on regional economic development. This is unfair to our regions here in Canada.

In addition to an interest rate that is too high, which means that we are using some 25 per cent of our money to pay off the national debt; in addition to spending a diminishing share of our national money on regional economic development, I also notice, in terms of fairness, that the Government estimates that it will be spending less on contributions to native economic development programs. I see the Minister responsible in the House. I wonder, in terms of fairness to our native, Indian, and aboriginal people, why the Government across the way is cutting down by about 8 per cent or some $6.25 million its contributions to native economic development programs.
We do not have fairness to our native people. We do not have fairness to the regions of the country. Finally, we do not have fairness in the Estimates in terms of older workers. There will be no new adjustments or designations of regions or industries for older workers. As a result of the February 1986 Budget the labour adjustment benefits program is gone, and older workers who were eligible for training are no longer getting the money they need in order to retrain. The new program which was announced, a program for older worker adjustment, still must receive some provincial-federal agreement, and therefore money is not being spent in that area. Thus older workers who are thrown on to the labour market have nowhere to turn in terms of retraining.
In conclusion, what we have before us today are the Estimates which will see us spending a greater and greater proportion of the Government's money, the taxpayers' money, the people's money in paying off the debt. The reason is that the Government across the way-and I am sure you share my concern, Mr. Speaker-has allowed the interest rate to get too high. If it would bring down the interest rate, we could save money and we could use that money in terms of regional economic development programs. This would be better for average Canadians or ordinary Canadians. It would mean
more fairness for each and everyone from one part of the country to another.

Mr. Speaker, we need and the Government of Canada needs new policies like this one.
I understand that in the Estimates, there is nothing at all to show an allocation of moneys for child care services. This, of course, was promised by certain Members across the way as recently as yesterday. That is another broken promise by the Government across the way which shows that it is a Government for the wealthy, for millionaires, for big shots and for big corporations. Years ago, my grandfather used to say that Tory times are tough times for ordinary Canadians, and they certainly are. It is the Party that brought us into the Dirty Thirties and it is the Party that once again is bringing regional inequity to this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
subsubtopic: REPORT OF MINISTER ON HER TRIP TO AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just returned from Ethiopia. I appreciate this opportunity to report to Members, at the earliest possible moment, on what is happening there, and what role Canada is playing ... More specifically, to share with you some of my findings ... and some of my feelings.
Whenever I travel to Africa, it is always a privilege to represent the Government and the people of Canada. Mr. Speaker, I am very proud of what we are doing in Africa.
And I was relieved and pleased to see many positive things in Ethiopia-our close cooperation with the people of that country ... the deep involvement of local people in the struggle for development. .. and encouraging signs of progress in the fight against famine.

My trip allowed me to meet with a wide variety of our partners. I met people from Canadian NGOs such as the World University Service of Canada, Canadian Physicians for Aid and Relief, the Sudan Interior Mission and McGill University as well as Ethiopian officials and senior representatives of United Nations agencies including Michael Priestley who is the special representative of the Secretary General of the United Nations, and the resident representative for the United Nations Development Program.
February 23, 1988



I had the opportunity to visit the north. At Mekele, 1 saw the food airlift in operation, and at the nearby settlement of Wukro, I watched the food being distributed.
What I saw in the north was, above all, the color brown- rough terrain, terrible roads, barren land, parched soil. .. everything brown, and incredibly dry. The earth, boiled and baked by the sun, was mere dust, dry and dead. But 1 also saw a very effective airlift hard at work, with Belgian hercules, Russian antonovs, small planes and helicopters all working together effectively.
I saw unloading operations at Mekele, and it was inspiring. Up to twenty big planes come in each day, bearing up to twenty tonnes of food per plane-much of it Canadian grain. I saw the hardworking teams of about eighteen Ethiopians who meet each plane and unload that twenty-tonne cargo into trucks, by hand, in as little as twelve minutes. Anyone who witnessed their energy and efficiency, under trying conditions, would never speak lightly about people not trying to help themselves.
At Wukro, I saw a well-organized food distribution effort, which was operating very smoothly. Non-governmental organizations-particularly medecins sans frontieres beiges- and the relief and rehabilitation commission were working closely together.
The names of recipients were recorded, village by village, on a register ... and checked off as the people collected their rations-thirty kilos per family member, enough for two months.
This time, Mr. Speaker, unlike 1984-85, people are taking the food back to their village-walking as far as fifty or sixty kilometres-rather than gathering in huge feeding camps at the distribution site.

Three years ago when famine struck, we saw images of despair and scenes of human suffering that haunted our minds: men and women reduced to skeletons and, the ultimate horror, children dying on camera. This time, though lives are certainly at risk, the condition of the people seems much better. In general, they appear to be in fair physical shape and in good spirits. It was encouraging to note that this time there is an organized baby-weighing program to detect signs of malnutrition.
Famine relief was not the only way I saw food aid being used. It is also serving the cause of longer-term development. Specifically, we visited a food-for-work project also at Wukro. Three thousand people are working with hand tools building earth dams about six metres high and 200 to 300 metres long. These dams will turn depressions in the terrain into reservoirs to hold the run off when the rains do come. The work of these
3,000	people is paid in food which keeps 3,000 families going, and at the same time, these people are creating a basic system to irrigate more than 70 hectares of land.
Tabling of Documents

I also went south, to Wanda Genet, and then to Awassa to visit a Canadian-sponsored water project. Mr. Speaker, I can report seeing much that gave me a feeling of relief-and of hope. I saw excellent cooperation between Canadians and Ethiopians-real involvement of the local communities in the projects-and fine work by NGOs (notably the Vancouver-based Hope International). True enough, I had seen evidence of these things in the north, too ... But in a setting where hostile nature and civil strife made progress virtually impossible.
In the south, the same factors, working in a more benign environment, were producing visible progress. I was very impressed by the degree of organization and determination shown by the Ethiopians. Their concern for the longer term was quite obvious-in, for instance, their creation of a water training institute. The most striking thing about the trip to the south was the physical contrast with conditions in the north. Brown gave way to green. We saw fertile land again. And we realized that, compared to the dry, brown north, other parts of Ethiopia have much better agricultural and water potential.
I am grateful to have had the opportunity to see for myself, first-hand, some of the realities of a most difficult and often tragic situation. I learned some valuable things-some of them cause for concern, others cause for hope and even a degree of satisfaction.
First, overall conditions are much better than in 1984-85. A good basic organization is in place to cope with the present emergency. In general, it is working effectively-although there are places, such as Korem, where it works less well.
Enough food is flowing into Ethiopia to prevent famine. Transport within Ethiopia, however, is another matter-in fact, a critical problem. The roads, where they exist, are poor to start with, and some are now impassable because they are increasingly unsafe. There are not enough trucks-many have been destroyed. There is not enough fuel-there is, for instance, none in place at the moment for the airlift. Planes have to detour to Addis Ababa to refuel, making the airlift even less efficient and more expensive as a way of carrying food-and yet it's the only way to stave off disaster.
Mr. Speaker, I learned yet again about the vital work being done by NGOs, and about the excellent level of cooperation with and among international organizations. I learned, once again, how much the world relies on the international committee of the Red Cross, which is playing a key role in this complex situation.
I saw with my own eyes that some parts of the country have extremely limited capacity to support life while other parts are fertile and productive. The rationale for Ethiopia's resettlement program, whatever the political motives, was undeniably

February 23, 1988
Tabling of Documents
visible and plain as day; brown dust in the north, green land in the south.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I was, and I remain, very concerned over persistent rumours of the use of force in the recently renewed resettlement campaign-even of shootings of people reluctant to move. Independent observers have attempted to verify these rumours on site-but so far there is no conclusive evidence to confirm or to refute the disturbing stories.
1 took every opportunity to make the position of Canada- and the international community, for that matter-crystal clear. I have been assured by the Ethopian government that Ethiopia's official policy, in the resumed program, is for voluntary resettlement only.

I can testify, Mr. Speaker, as a firsthand witness that Canada is playing a valuable and significant part in helping to avoid a huge tragedy in Ethiopia. We did much in 1984-85. We are doing still more this time, and the Government of Canada will always be ready to aid the victims of disaster, whether the disaster is natural or man made. I can report that Canadians, along with people from many other countries, are doing marvellous work under the most difficult conditions, and I feel obliged to say that our continued help and support is a matter of life and death to millions of people whose future hangs on a precarious, knife-edge balance.
These few words can express only a fraction of my thoughts and feelings as I saw, briefly, the ordeal of the people of Ethiopia and the spirit of their struggle to survive and move ahead.
[ Translation]
In closing, Mr. Speaker, 1 will just mention that, on leaving Ethiopia, I proceeded to Bamako, to take part in the fifth bilateral consultation between Canada and Mali. I was able to visit one of the many excellent grassroots projects under way there, and to have good discussions on the difficult problems facing Mali and the other countries of the Sahel. And the meeting allowed me, on African soil, to assure the people of that country and that continent, once again, of the continuing concern and support they can count on, from the government, the parliament and the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MINISTER ON HER TRIP TO AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I want to say that I regret that I was not in receipt of a copy of the Minister's address until a very short time before the House began. Such an important subject deserves a worthy commentary from our Party and 1 do regret that we did not receive the text of this speech until such a late hour.
However, having said that, I want to express on behalf of our Party and of all Members of the House our sincere appreciation to the Minister for External Relations (Mrs.
Landry) for having herself gone to see firsthand the circumstances and the problems facing the people of Ethiopia and the problems facing those who are trying to do something about the tragedies that are taking place. Her visit is to be commended. We also appreciate her report in the House making it the business of all of us to be concerned about the events taking place in Ethiopia.
We are also proud of the role Canada is playing. The Minister pointed out that we are taking a very vigorous role. Our NGOs as well as our government officials are actively trying to do what they can. It was also stirring to hear the Minister tell us that many countries from around the world are working together. Instead of seeing our allies coming together to fight against other nations in war we see them coming together from both sides to war against this tragedy of hunger and famine. Those are all positive things. I hope my comments will be understood in the context of my congratulations to the Minister and also in the context of being pleased to hear the positive aspects of her report.
We have much to be thankful for that things are not in the same state and condition they were several years ago when famine struck Ethiopia and the world was caught quite flatfooted and fairly unaware. The media brought to our attention so effectively and valuably the horrors and starvation facing the Ethiopians. Now that the media aroused us to that kind of common concern, questions must be discussed and I want to raise these questions in the House as part of our concern.
We are told by the Minister that right now enough food is flowing into Ethiopia to prevent famine, that is, enough food is on hand. But the Minister goes on to point out that the problem of trying to transport the food to where the people are is horrendous. It appears that the solution is not to take the food to where the people are where their homes are, where their communities and traditions are but rather to bring the people to where the food is, namely, at the depots. That seems a little strange. It is quite obvious that one clear reason is that there is drought in the north and in the areas of Eritrea and we know that in northern Ethiopia as the Minister pointed out there is brown dirt, drought and, therefore, famine, and in the south it is greener.
Regrettably there are other dynamics at play. We know there is a guerilla war going on, a revolution, or a fight for independence, whichever way you want to put it and on whose side you happen to be sitting, but the people in Eritrea and Tigre are people who are concerned about their own independence and their ability to have freedom and to have their own way of life.
This war which goes on between the Government of Ethiopia and the rebels, or the people who are seeking independence, is also tragic. In the course of this war which has been going on for many years we know that people have been brought forcefully, resettled from the north, into Ethiopia in order to take away the bases of supply for the rebels. We know that horrendous violations of human rights have taken
February 23, 1988

place-some would even say a form of genocide in years gone-on the part of the Ethiopians against the people in that area in their so-called resettlement efforts. The Minister, however, is assuring us today. She says she is hopeful that this will not take place in future resettlement patterns, and I am hopeful as well. But we are confronted by a serious question as to whether these resettlement programs can be really said to be only a matter of trying to deal with the matter of bringing the people to the food and away from the drought areas, or whether also there are certain other factors in place that involve military and other political concerns on the part of the Ethiopian Government.
What is the Minister and the Department of External Affairs going to do about these problems? Flave we in the West, the more affluent countries with much wealth and power, really done enough in advance? Canada has such great abilities in transportation. Flave we in the past tried to ensure better transportation systems? Is there anything we could have done about it? That is a very important question in light of the danger of starvation and the tragedy of resettlement which is at hand.
What are we doing to monitor the human rights situation of these people? The Minister says that there is a voluntary resettlement program. How voluntary can a resettlement program really be when army trucks drive up to a community and load people up telling them that they are going south or they will starve, that there will be no food coming in? How voluntary is such a resettlement program? How much choice do they have? That is another question we must ask ourselves searchingly.
Can Canada, with all of its ability in the field of helping out, not use some of its influence to monitor the human rights of those people? What program do we have in place to monitor human rights?
There is an underlying question. What is the Department of External Affairs doing in terms of diplomacy to try to bring the world together. We can bring food together in such a wonderful way, but what are we doing to bring the world together through the United Nations or other ways to solve quickly the tragic war that is taking place in Ethiopia? Are we showing the same kind of energetic leadership as we are showing in the field of humanitarian concern to try to bring about a solution to this tragedy in Ethiopia? Can nations as powerful as the United States, the Soviet Union, Canada, France, Britain, China and India not bring a quick solution to the suffering that is caused in large measure by the tragic problems which exist as a result of the guerrilla war and the constant conflict? Can we not step in more energetically?
These are the kinds of questions which I think Canadians would want to address to the Minister. In appreciation for her report and in thanksgiving for the things that are being done,
Tabling of Documents
we yet have to ask these questions searchingly. We hope to hear from her further in response.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MINISTER ON HER TRIP TO AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of my colleagues, the Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) and the Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), I am pleased to rise today on behalf of the New Democratic Party to respond to the Minister's statement.
With respect to the specifics of the latter, I would like to start by saying that we on this side of the House are genuinely concerned by the prospect that millions of Ethiopians are again facing starvation. Canadians must respond. The question is how.

When we try to fight famine in Ethiopia, we must realize that famine and the political situation are very closely linked. Granted, drought and gradual desertification are the main causes, but it is also true that the victims of these natural disasters are too often manipulated and used as bait both by the Government and the rebels who are locked in a struggle to control the country. We, and in fact all Canadians find this state of affairs abhorrent.
Hunger knows no politics, and we cannot let food be used as an instrument to control people. The Canadian Government and the international community must state clearly to the two forces who are locked in confrontation that Ethiopians who are dying of hunger must not be used as hostages.

Canadians believe that the larger and more serious problems of hunger and starvation cannot be ignored and must be addressed. In this respect Canadian aid programs need to consider two interrelated problems; what can be done to alleviate the critical hunger crisis facing Ethiopia today, and what can we do to alleviate the longer-term problems at the root of the current crisis?
Insofar as the immediate crisis is concerned, we believe that Canada must continue its emergency food and medical relief efforts in order to avoid another tragedy like the one we witnessed in 1984-85. I am sure everyone in this House would share that sentiment. Where the problems arise, however, is in ensuring that our humanitarian aid reaches those most in need rather than being used for political or military purposes.
I would have hoped that the Minister would have had more concrete measures to report in this regard. In particular, she should have outlined to this House and to the Canadian people what action the Canadian Government is prepared to undertake to ensure that Canadian and, indeed, all humanitarian aid is guaranteed free and unhindered access to the needy in all parts of Ethiopia; that relief convoys are clearly identifiable as such and that verification procedures are implemented to ensure that such convoys are not used for military purposes; that food assistance and logistical support are not used directly

February 23, 1988
Petitions
or indirectly for forced resettlement and villagization programs; and that food relief is not misappropriated for military forces. I think the Minister's statement would have been more useful and reassuring to Canadians if she had addressed some of these substantive issues.
With regard to the longer-term undertakings necessary to try to reverse the current cycle of famine and starvation in Ethiopia, we believe that we need to move away from the current large mega-project approach and focus more of our attention and money on smaller local aid programs geared to the population's needs and capabilities. This shift in emphasis has been under discussion for some time and 1 think it would be helpful, for both Ethiopia and other nations, if the Minister would finally announce the long promised new CIDA policy that so many have for so long been waiting. Unfortunately, this new policy appears to have become bogged down in Cabinet. I would like to take this opportunity to urge the Minister and her cabinet colleagues to finally outline to this House and to the country what new and hopefully decentralized CIDA policy they have in mind.
The current cycle of famine and starvation places great strains on the aid community's efforts to address the longer-term structural, agricultural and environmental problems at the heart of the problem in Ethiopia. I would caution, however, that this dilemma should not be looked at primarily as a question of the allocation of scarce financial resources. In this regard we believe that our longer-term projects should not be allowed to suffer in order to find the funds necessary to respond to current or future hunger crises. Instead, I would argue that each and every famine situation requires an infusion of significant new funds to meet the immediate threat so that many of our longer-term projects can proceed relatively unhindered. Otherwise we are merely engaged in band-aid solutions that will ultimately do little to alleviate the suffering in Ethiopia.
[ Translation]
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk about the problem of the Ethiopian government's population displacement program. Initially, the purpose of the program was to move residents of famine-stricken areas to the southern part of the country where the land is more fertile. However, the program has become very controversial. The Ethiopian government's approach is clumsy and dictatorial. Its intentions are far more political than humanitarian. It seems that residents of the North are being forced to move to more southerly regions which, unfortunately, are not ready to receive them.
Last week, as the Minister herself reported, there were rumours that the Ethiopian army had shot twenty people who refused to take part in the program. The Minister must try and find out whether these allegations are true.
It is also said that camps in the North, the same camps that are receiving supplies from international agencies, are being used by the Ethiopian government as transit centres for its massive displacement programs. With all these allegations, the
Canadian Government is in a very uncomfortable situation. Only two countries are helping to facilitate these moves, and Canada is one of them. With these persistent rumours, the question arises whether Canada should continue to help the Ethiopian government displace all these people.
Insofar as it concerns the Canadian Government sponsored resettlement programs in Ethiopia which are run by NGO's and not the Ethiopian Government, there seems to be evidence that the result has been an appreciable improvement in living conditions. However, other resettlement programs may not have been as beneficial.
In addition, irrespective of the relative benefit of any particular resettlement program, we cannot support the forced deportation of starving Ethiopians to resettlement areas, Canadian or otherwise. As such, I welcome the Minister's statement that any resettlement program must be strictly voluntary.
However, I must also point out that she has again failed to outline exactly what steps she plans to implement to ensure that resettlement to Canadian sponsored resettlement areas or any resettlement area is done on a purely voluntary basis. Without such a clear outline of practices, guidelines and verification procedures, I fear the Minister's statement may in fact turn out to be more rhetorical than real. Once again, the Minister should have been more forthcoming on specifics.
I want to join with my Liberal colleague in recognizing the fact that it is the war, insurrection, or revolution in Ethiopia that has caused much of the difficulty we face in ensuring that aid is properly distributed in that country. I join with him, as I am sure will others in the House, in asking the Government to pursue whatever means and agencies it can find, with other nations through the UN or elsewhere, to ensure that peace is brought to Ethiopia soon as a result of international cooperation in that regard.

speechtext:

The Conservative Government is cheering so hard for the haves in our society that it is unable to hear the cries of those who have not been able to benefit from an improved economy. And, Mr. Speaker, one of the regions that has not benefited from this improved economy is the very riding I happen to represent.
Mr. Speaker, the day after the Budget, the Reeve of Cambridge Township in my riding, who happens to be Chairman of the ITAC (Industry, Tourism, Agriculture and Commerce) Committee of the United Counties of Prescott and Russell, issued a press release containing his views on the Budget. As you know, Mr. Speaker, and as I am sure many Members of the House know, Glengarry-Prescott-Russell is not a rich constituency. The western part of the constituency is made up mostly of civil servants. There are many farmers throughout the greater part of my constituency. TThere are small industrial towns in the eastern part of it as well. There are 25 municipalities and some 50 small towns.
The gas tax that was included in the Budget is most unfair to my rural constituents. They do not have a choice with respect to whether or not they should own an automobile. If one wants to work in a rural area then one has to find a means of getting to one's job. That means is usually an automobile. That automobile must have its tank filled with gas in order to run. People filling their tanks are now paying a higher level for
February 23, 1988

gas than they have ever paid. This is from a Government which promised prior to the 1984 election not to increase taxes. Since the Government was sworn into office gas taxes have increased 5 cents per litre. That comes out to 23 cents per gallon.

The problem is with the long distance phone charges since almost every phone call one makes is a long distance phone call.	[DOT]

For my constituents the problem is not with the basic rate, it is with the long distance phone charges which are too expensive already.
Some communities in my riding which are just on the outskirts of Ottawa have to pay long distance charges in order to phone the city. That is another matter and it is unfair. It is unfair for the people of Plantagenet, the people of Casselman, Clarence Creek and Bourget to pay long distance charges at all to phone Ottawa. and all Canadians willing to listen to him, and their number is getting increasingly smaller, that one of the great benefits of the Free Trade Agreement would be that the customs tariffs would go down and that Canadian consumers would be able to purchase products made in the United States at a lower price than those made in Canada. Yet, Mr. Speaker, we have learned differently in the recent Budget. At first glance, this seems like a bargain as Canadians will pay $460 million less. However, the facts disprove this. The Government has increased the tax on gasoline to collect an additional $300 million in revenue, which amount approaches that of the revenues lost because of the lower tariffs under the trade agreement.
Mr. Speaker, in other words, all Canadians, including the constituents of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, especially those in rural areas, will have to pay 1 cent a litre more in taxes on gasoline this year to pay for the Free Trade Agreement of the Prime Minister.

The Budget-Mrs. McDougall
increased only by 28 per cent, or half the increase which applies to individual Canadians.

A one-earner family of four with an income of $32,00 a year is now paying $1,200 more in taxes. That family, not having had a salary increase at all for the last four years, actually end up with $1,200 less than before the Government came into office.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Budget of February 10 is a plan designed to create two Canadas and two solitudes: A nation of privileged Canadians who enjoy prosperity while the poorest and neediest will suffer even more.
My colleagues in the Liberal Party and myself believe that Canada is a generous nation and that all Canadians will reject the cynical budgetary plan of the Minister of Finance and the Conservative Party.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin by quoting from our Government's agenda for economic renewal which all Hon. Members will recall was presented to the House November 8, 1984:
We have set four challenges:
first, to put our own fiscal house in order so that we can limit, and ultimately reverse, the massive build-up in public debt and the damaging impact this has on confidence and growth;
second, to redefine the role of government so that it provides a better framework for growth and job creation and less of an obstacle to change and innovation;
third, to foster higher investment, greater innovation, increased international competitiveness and a positive climate for the birth and growth of new enterprise; and
fourth, to bring about these changes in a way that is fair, open and consistent with the basic sense of compassion, tolerance and justice that is characteristic of Canadian society.
Those were our four challenges after 25 years of Liberal profligacy, spending everything they could lay their hands on. Let us look at how we lived up to these commitments.

Our first commitment was to set our financial house in order. By 1985 the federal deficit and the national debt were practically out of control, and everyone suffers when a government loses control over its finances. It invariably leads to higher rates for mortgages as well as for corporate and consumer loans, economic faith vanishes, growth stops, and jobs get ever scarcer. That is what we inherited from the previous Liberal administration.
We believe that Canadians want their children and grandchildren to look forward to a promising and challenging future instead of saddling them with crushing debts and lost hopes.
The only way to prepare for this kind of future is to devise a medium-term financial plan geared to a steady deficit decline, and to stick to that plan.

That is exactly what we have done through a series of actions. Our first priority had to be to get government spending under control. In the four years prior to our coming into office, spending on programs had increased at an average annual rate of 14 per cent. Fourteen per cent! That is way ahead of the rate of inflation, enough to double spending in about five years. Since 1984 we have cut the average annual rate of increase in Government spending to just 3.5 per cent, less than the rate of inflation. We achieved this record because we put in place a new and disciplined approach to the management of Government and its finances.
We said that control of expenditures would be the main source of deficit reduction, and it has been. For the current fiscal year we said that we would cut the deficit to $29.3 billion, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has said that he will meet that target. Our Government has met every deficit reduction target that it has set. I need not remind Hon. Members of the very poor planning of previous Governments that never could meet a target.
We said that we would respond to the priorities and the real needs of Canadians in a fiscally responsible way, and we have done so. When we came into office there is no question that sound financial management was essential. It is essential now, and it will be essential in the future. It is a fact of life. It is a fiscal principle that we will adhere to.
First, we are reducing the growth rate of the national debt to no more than that of the economy by 1990-91, that massive debt that was accumulated under the Liberals. Second, we are achieving steady year-to-year declines in the deficit. The reduction projected for 1988-89 will be the first time in the post-war period that the deficit has declined four years in a row. Third, we are ensuring substantial reductions in the Government's financial requirements. Fourth, we are achieving the greater part of this progress through expenditure restraint and disciplined management. Our fiscal principles and structural improvements will ensure that we stay on our fiscal course.
Our next commitment on the agenda was to change the role of Government intervention in order to foster a climate for job creation. We recognize that the driving force behind productive growth, new jobs, is a dynamic private sector. In order to facilitate this growth our Government has undertaken many measures that have resulted in record job increases.

We have deregulated the energy and transport sectors. We have opened the financial markets to world-wide opportunities and emphasized even stronger competition in financial services. We have set up Investment Canada with a view to
February 23, 1988

promoting and welcoming foreign investment in this country, the kind of investment which create jobs for Canadians.

For the corporate sector many special tax breaks thoughtlessly introduced previously are being eliminated or reduced, and tax rates are being lowered. That means our corporate tax system for small businesses and others will be more competitive with those in other countries. But there is, of course, more to be done.
We are going to replace an archaic federal sales tax system with a multi-stage system which will be effective in supporting growth and job creation, and it will be fair. We have been working with the provinces and others to develop the most effective means of implementing this new system, particularly the opportunity to have an integrated national sales tax. So far progress with the provinces has been good, but we do have more work to do.
Let us look at where all this has led-massive job creation. Let us look at the record. First, contrary to all the constant whining from the other side of the Flouse, employment under this Government has risen in every single province in Canada. That translates into 1.156 million new jobs; people who are working today who were not working in September, 1984. Those are not only temporary or part-time jobs, as was the case with the previous Government. Eighty-five per cent of these new jobs are full time. The Liberals created only 87,000 full-time jobs in 55 months. Our Government has seen to the creation of 978,000 full-time jobs in only 40 months.
In my home town, if I may be allowed to discuss the City of Toronto and the good people of St. Paul's, unemployment is only 4.4 per cent and 181,000 new jobs have been created since 1984.

speechtext:
I am about to explain that to the Hon. Member, Mr. Speaker, if she is prepared to listen.
The Budget-Mrs. McDougall
A large portion of those jobs, 50 per cent, have been in managerial, professional, and administrative positions. I do not need to remind the women of Canada that their unemployment rate rose by 3.4 per cent under the previous Liberal Government, and most of those jobs were part-time. This is a solid record of progress. It illustrates how our policies and our approaches work.
Our third commitment on the agenda for economic renewal, Members may recall, was to create policies to increase our international competitiveness and innovation. That we have done in three ways. Earlier I mentioned Investment Canada, and that has resulted in new job opportunities for Canadians. It has been a part of the success that we have had since taking office. We are also moving on two other fronts of enormous significance to Canadians, first, the multilateral trade negotiations under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and, of course, the free trade agreement with the United States.
Our Government recognizes the dangers in protectionism in other countries, and we are pushing hard for reforms to reduce protectionist policies in those trading nations involved in the GATT. It is important for our Government to continue to work hard to this end, but it is also important to remember that there are more than 90 nations involved in this process. It takes a great deal of time, a great deal of discipline, and sometimes some compromise among such a large number of nations. That is why we decided to pursue an agreement with our largest trading partner, the United States. The free trade agreement is a major building block in the Government's strategy to strengthen Canada's competitive position, not only with the United States but in the world, and to enhance the prosperity of our people.
Canadian producers will now have access to a market of 270 million people. Canadian consumers will benefit from more competitive prices on a wider variety of goods, and both countries will be able to appeal unfair trade practices to an appeal panel. Those are important breakthroughs in the world's largest trading relationship, and breakthroughs that are being watched with great interest by other trading partners in the world. They also mean greater opportunity and prosperity for Canadians.
There are many cases. There was one profiled yesterday in a Toronto newspaper, Mr. Speaker, the The Globe and Mail, where a manufacturing company in Guelph, Ontario will spend $9 million on capital expenditures next year to gear up for free trade. The company stated that the $9 million would not have been spent without this agreement. These are real opportunities, real growth, real industrial expansion, and this will lead to real jobs, despite all the noise and rhetoric from the other side.
Ever since October I have been travelling across Canada talking to many Canadians about free trade. I have been struck by the amount of support for the agreement from two particular groups, the first being Canadian entrepreneurs.

February 23, 1988
The Budget-Mr. E. Epp
They are very anxious for this agreement. When I asked a friend why they were not out making speeches on behalf of themselves and their companies, he said that they were not doing it because they were too busy getting ready. The second group with which I am particularly impressed is our young people-the future of our country. They are embracing this arrangement with enthusiasm. They are enthusiastic about the opportunity to compete and to have a prosperous future. They want this agreement.
Finally, our fourth commitment on the agenda for economic renewal is to bring about these changes in a way that is fair, open, and consistent with the characteristics of our Canadian society. By creating more jobs, more opportunities, and better incomes, the Government enhances its ability to do more for Canadians and to have Canadians do more for themselves, and we have done more.

1 am extremely proud of the national day care strategy recently unveiled by our Government, a series of initiatives through which $5.4 billion will be channelled towards our most precious resource, our children. The approach we took gives every consideration to the various options facing families, according to their own preferences and circumstances. By means of tax credits and other incentives we will help parents who want to avail themselves of outside day care services or who would rather provide such services at home.
We have also set up a $100 million fund for special initiatives which will enable us to establish new programs for children in particular situations, including smaller localities and rural areas. We will soon release more details concerning this program.

We have expanded the spousal allowance to widowed persons between the ages of 60 and 64 years. We have improved the Canada Pension Plan and veterans' pensions, and we have provided assistance to the disabled.
In response to the current situation facing agricultural producers, federal government expenditures in agriculture will increase from $1.2 billion last year to over $4 billion this year.
The Government has also taken far-reaching measures to reform the federal tax system, a system which had reached a dreadful state of affairs when we took over. We are making the tax system fairer for individual Canadians. We are making it more effective in supporting job creation and growth. We are creating a system which helps our small businesses and industries to compete in the world. For individuals we are replacing 10 tax brackets with three. To make the system fairer we are converting personal exemptions and many deductions to tax credits, and we are reducing and eliminating many special tax breaks.
The results are substantial. More than eight out of ten households will see their personal income taxes reduced. Some
850,000	lower income individuals will have their income tax reduced to zero. Almost nine out of ten Canadians aged 65 years and over will have income tax reductions. The vast majority of families with children will pay noticeably less personal income tax.
We will continue the course set out three and a half years ago, because we know that it is right and Canadians know that it is working. As the Minister of Finance stated in The Budget Speech, "there are no short cuts to achieving Canada's economic potential".
We are heading into a new century and, as we approach its last decade, Canadians-men, women, and young people-are ready and confident. Every time a key is turned in the door of a new business, a new home, or a new factory, that confidence is shown. We are seeing more of that every day under this Government. Every time a kid passes an exam, a young couple gets married, or a family chooses Canada as their new home, it is an expression of that confidence. As a country we do not take a back seat to anybody. Government policies must reflect the confidence which Canadians have in themselves and the pride they have in our country.
These initiatives and others like them are why Canadians elected a Progressive Conservative Government in 1984. It is the reason that I am very proud to be a member of the Government. It is the record on which Canadians will vote in the next election when they re-elect a Progressive Conservative Government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to join this afternoon in the debate on the very thin budget speech which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) read on the afternoon of February 10. It was a speech full of election rhetoric and the kind of complacency which the Minister of State for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs (Mrs. McDougall) has just served up in her speech. It is the kind of pleasure people feel when they represent St. Paul's or other ridings in the metropolitan area, when they look around and see unemployment rates down to 4 per cent, when they think that all is well with the country and that their program is succeeding. They think that they simply have to stay the course and the Canadian people will re-elect them to serve up more of the high unemployment which so many regions of Canada still know, the kind of taxation which has been dumped on average and low-income Canadians over the past three years, and the kind of taxation which allows the Government to talk now about reduction of taxes for this same mass of Canadians.
Of course one can reduce taxes somewhat if one is loading thousands of dollars more on the average family. Of course one could achieve some reduction after having done so, but that is hardly real cause for complacency.
February 23, 1988

Government Members will regret the fact that election after election they served up that kind of inequity and that they ignored so much of the country in the way they have. We have commentators wondering these days whether they will make a serious try to win seats in the Metropolitan Toronto area. If they cannot win them there, they are certainly not going to win them in other parts of the country where they have done nasty things to people, ignored the regions, and neglected again in this Budget to recognize what the country needs, to take up the challenge, and to provide the kind of leadership the country wants.
What we have as a reality in much of the country is unemployment rates which are still, in eight of the ten provinces, very close to the levels they reached in the recession or the interest rate depression of the early eighties, from 1981 to 1983. There is no reason for complacency.
They have failed to come to grips with these matters or to take action for regions of the country which so desperately need it, other than press releases and the flackery of an Atlantic Opportunities Agency that is still not funded, a western development organization that is still more structure than activity, and a northern Ontario initiative that is still busy developing application forms.
This hiving off of responsibilities for the regions, which has marked the Government's policy over the last couple of years, deserves very critical and careful examination. I suspect that what it actually reveals is the constraint or the strait-jacket that the Government is taking on even before the free trade agreement has been passed by the U.S. Congress or adopted by the Canadian Parliament. It is a consequence of this action of tying Canada to the United States in so many ways.
I make that argument because we realize very well that the attack of the Americans-the American people, American industries, politicians, or U.S. administration-to facilitate the process carried out on Canadian industries was very often focused on development programs or regional development initiatives that encouraged those industries. The Government has accepted, in its free trade agreement, and not having had any success in that area, a five-year to seven-year process of negotiating its way through these matters. What the Government is desperately afraid of is that any kind of initiatives that it takes on these matters in the regions will be attacked by the American partner in this trade deal.
[DOT] (BOO)
Recognizing that, what the Government has done is to put the responsibility on agencies, leaving them some money which will be in their control, not really in Ottawa's control; $3 billion has been pulled out of regional development reducing the amount that is actually spent in the hope that this will get us past the American attacks on government programs in Canada. The end result is that the Government is left hoping that the free market, to which it pays its respects time after time, the lower interest rates, for which it has precious little
The Budget-Mr. E. Epp
responsibility, will continue to allow the creation of jobs that has taken place over the last three years. Unfortunately that situation has not occurred in much of the country. In northern Ontario where my constituents live and in other regions, unemployment rates still remain very very high.
If we have a government that continues on the course which this Government has taken in the trade deal negotiation with the U.S., I do not see any way out. It only underscores our criticism of the deal, our opposition to it, and our need to find a different framework. We need desperately to come up with an economic policy that will allow us to achieve full employment in the regions of Canada and to move the country toward the balanced budget that all of us would like to see. If we are going to do that, we will have to move away from this preoccupation the Government has with deficit reduction; first and foremost with the loading on of higher taxes in a completely unbalanced way, and with the focus on the trade deal that I have already pointed out.
We might note that in all the advocacy for the trade deal which the Conservatives have put forward, the actual number of jobs we are supposed to get out of it over half a decade-or perhaps it is over 10 years-as a net result, is a very small number. One hundred and twenty thousand jobs is the net gain which is less than half of what lower interest rates allowed Canadians to achieve year by year since 1983. Fully realizing, even if the Minister of State for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs does not want to admit it in public, that there will be massive dislocations in the Canadian economy and thousands of jobs will be lost in the various industries with only the hope that the theoretical results to flow from freer trade will, in fact, bring us more employment, we are faced with the possibility that even the hope for 120,000 jobs as the net gain is a doubtful projection.
If one looks at all of that and recognizes the dislocations that will occur, the limitations the Government has accepted in the free trade agreement in dealing with those things, I can understand why the Minister does not want to admit that the Government should take action. The result for thousands of Canadians will be even more of the distress we have already known.
What should be have in these circumstances? I suggest we should be looking to opportunities within Canada as much as outside. Certainly Canadians want to trade. New Democrats are supportive of trade with the United States in our various industries, as is anyone, from the raw materials to the achievements of the automotive industry and high technology. But opportunities within Canada deserve to be emphasized, and challenges within this country as well. We want to look toward achieving full employment in every region and not be content with it in southern Ontario, particularly in the golden horseshoe and around metro Toronto.
We should be looking at a policy of fair taxation in which the burden of expenditure by the federal Government and other Governments is fairly distributed. Those who have the

February 23, 1988
The Budget-Mr. E. Epp
wealth and the income should shoulder that burden much more fairly than is now the case. Particularly looking at fairness, we should be looking to a rebalancing from individuals to corporations so that all recipients of income-and corporations so often receive income but do not distribute it- share in tax paying far more than is now the case. All should share in carrying the burden, meeting the challenges and seeing the promise of Canada achieved.
In this policy, we should be recognizing the importance of lower interest rates and pressing the Governor of the Bank of Canada to get those interest rates down. There are only the first suspicions of this developing these days, but the Bank of Canada is maintaining a policy of fighting inflation. The governor actually suggests reducing inflation to zero which strikes me quite incredible. A dynamic private sector uses price increases as one of its responses to the market. Achieving zero inflation will have incredible costs for Canadians, the kinds of costs which the United States federal reserve system imposed on much of the world in the early 1980s. If the Governor of the Bank of Canada is going to maintain that kind of course he will ruin the country.
Why would the Minister of Finance and the Government tolerate that? Are they again, because of the free trade agreement, encouraging the governor to keep interest rates high in order to have the value of the dollar appreciate? The dollar has increased in value by pretty close to 10 per cent in the last little while against the U.S. dollar. That increase of 10 per cent strikes Americans, who are competing with Canadian producers in their market, as a real advantage. Canadian products become more expensive. Those who saw the lower valued dollar at 72 cents, or whatever value it was in the last little while, saw that as a Canadian Government subsidy and could very well think that the Canadian Government, Mr. Crowe at the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance, are involved in raising the value of the dollar through higher interest rates to reduce one more subsidy, so-called, to Canadian industry. These are the kinds of charges by the United States that should be forthrightly met rather than yielded to.
It is all the more important to deal with this and to get those interest rates down when we recognize what lower interest rates have made possible in the last several years. As I suggested before, we have seen something like 300,000 jobs created by Canadians year by year for the last several years. The main reason is that interest rates have been at a reasonable level. The American authorities recognized that what they did in the early 1980s could destroy the world, bringing about a global depression, and they have backed off.
It has been possible to carry on housing construction again. Industries have been prepared to invest. We have seen new plants established and so on. All of these things have made a
300,000	person year increase in employment in Canada. It is that kind of possibility within this country which within one year gives us more jobs than the trade deal the Government
holds out promises over a decade. That indicates the importance of lower interest rates and other domestic policies to achieve full employment.
The fact that we still have about one million Canadians unemployed, and there are still about as many people unemployed now as have found jobs over the last three or four years, is an indication of the challenge we find in the various regions of Canada. If we had the interest rate reductions that we should have, one or two percentage points now, to bring interest rates closer to American rates, such a reduction would have a significant impact. It would have an impact first on the Estimates of the Government, which were tabled this morning, and on the finances of the country. A 1 per cent drop in interest rates on government financial obligations would save the Minister of Finance over $1.3 billion in a year. That is certainly a saving to make when there are so many needs, so many calls on the Government, in various regions of the country. It would also bring the cost of establishing businesses in Canada closer to the American level. Interest rates that are 30 per cent to 40 per cent above American interest rates clearly represent a penalty on Canadian industry and it is the very opposite of a subsidy. This is an additional cost which Canadian industry faces when it wants to compete with American industry. There is a second very sound reason for reducing the interest rate.
Of course, over the last three years, Canadian consumers have played an important part in the return to some prosperity in certain parts of the country and in some reduction in the unemployment rate in various places including my community where housing construction has been an important factor. The fact that consumers have been able to buy houses again is surely a factor of lower interest rates. I would suggest, particularly after the crash of last October and the impact that has had on the North American economy and the U.S. economy particularly, an impact that is being felt in Canada bit by bit, it would be very important to have a reduction in interest rates.
I think these observations suggest to us that in the fiscal and monetary policies the Government is following in its Budget, the Minister of Finance failed to come to grips with the challenge. He is prepared to let the resource hinterland of the United States, which a continental energy deal would suggest, be a basic feature of his view of Canada. Of course, he thinks there will be more industrial opportunities thanks to the trade agreement, but no one can be really sure of that. There are many questions about that.
The possibility of a Canada that is well developed, prosperous and balanced, a country in which taxation is fair so that lower and middle-income Canadians do not bear the mammoth burden they do now, is a possibility toward which changes should be made. The Minister of Finance has failed to do that. He has failed to recognize the importance of supporting prosperity across the country, of building up all the regions.
February 23, 1988

Fie has failed to realize the importance of initiatives by the federal Government that would assist the movement toward full employment in northern Ontario, across the West, in Quebec and in Atlantic Canada.
I think of our infrastructure needs. One such need in particular has become very important for us in northern Ontario, and that is improvements to the Trans-Canada Highway which is now a quarter century old. Quite clearly, it is inadequate to the challenge, particularly in the context of trucking deregulation. The Canadian Government is supporting highway construction in every Province of Canada but Ontario. It is supporting construction on the Yellowhead Highway in the West, of all things, not even the Trans-Canada. It is under pressure these days in New Brunswick and in Ontario to take up the challenge of improving significant sections of the Trans-Canada Highway. We in northern Ontario have a quarter of the total kilometres of the Trans-Canada Highway.
A Government that is prepared to look to the market and thinks that agreements with the United States will do it, a Government that is prepared to be complacent about the rest, given the prosperity in the Metro-Toronto area, is a Government that ignores these particular challenges. It ignores the needs of the regions which, if met, could produce better employment.
I can think of other needs for municipal infrastructure. More particularly, in northern Ontario, some of the new Indian reserves should be developed, reserves on which the Government is refusing to spend any money. These are needs that would support the prosperity of the communities and move us closer to full employment. These are real Canadian needs. Meeting them would support the good health and the safety of the Canadian people. These are actions the Government should be taking. However, there has been no such action.
There has been an obsession with the market and with the U.S. tie-in. This obsession is likely to bring us incredible uncertainties over the next years, incredible dislocations and losses of jobs. Maybe there will be some net gains at the end, but there is no assurance of that. The Government has failed to recognize the challenges which face us. It has failed to take up those challenges. That is why in the regions of the country, province after province, this Government will be defeated in the next election so that other people who recognize the need to get on with the job will actually do it.
