speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my socialist colleague from Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp). He says the Budget is unrealistic and does not reflect the real situation in this country. However, in his speech he failed to mention how his party, if it had to make the decisions and prepare a budget, would improve the lives of Canadians. I could find nothing in his speech that gave any indication of the approach his party would take. He says he would reduce unemployment,
The Budget-Mr. E. Epp
but he fails to say how. He says he would increase services to Canadians, but he doesn't say how. He says he would reduce taxes, but he doesn't say how. I would appreciate it if the Hon. Member, in the few minutes he has left, would consider this essential part he left out of his speech and inform Canadians what he would do if he were Minister of Finance and what kind of action he would take.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question. In 20 minutes one can do so little. 1 think 1 did more than he has suggested, but I appreciate an opportunity to expand somewhat.
I was suggesting that we want to achieve a full-employment and a balanced-Budget Canada, a Canada in which we would be able to begin paying off some of the national debt rather than being obsessed with deficit reduction. We want to do that through a number of different actions. We want to reduce interest rates in order to encourage economic activity and reduce the cost of Government. I think I said enough about that so I will not expand on it.
We want to have a fair tax system, a tax system in which some of the burden is taken off individual Canadians. Once upon a time, within our lifetimes, as a matter of fact, the tax balance between individuals and corporations was more or less fifty-fifty. That was back in the 1950s. But over the years, particularly through the 1970s when the Liberals were in charge and the present Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) was Minister of Finance, things began to go badly awry. Corporations ceased to pay as much as individuals. By now, of course, individuals pay four and four and a half times as much.
I would suggest that real tax reform would get things back into balance and would reduce taxes for individual Canadians. That real tax reform supports economic activity and allows corporations to achieve profits and pay the taxes, something which they might not like initially but which would be quite bearable, given the prosperity that would follow from tax reduction. After lower interest rates, that could be the most dynamic and explosive force the Canadian economy could achieve.
When we move toward full employment, we should get budgets that are closer to balanced. When the Auditor General's Office tells us that if the Canadian economy currently were in full employment, the Budget would still be in the red by perhaps $8 billion, we can see a measure of how unbalanced and unfortunate the Canadian tax system actually is. We simply have to come to grips with bearing the load in a balanced way, not by dumping it on individual Canadians as this Government has done even more than the Liberals did before. We need to get this into balance. Having achieved that, we would then spend our money carefully in order to encourage the move toward full employment, whether it be spent on infrastructure improvements or on post-secondary education and health. Year after year, we have seen pressures to hold

February 23, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Ferland
back in those areas. After 10 to 15 years of inadequate funding in these areas, one wonders how many thousands of jobs could be created by doing these things properly.
These days, Ontario universities are very anxious because there is a 10 per cent increase in applications for next year. How can these applications be managed when the Canadian Government is not doing its share and the provincial Government is failing in the same way?
We have challenge after challenge to be met. As we do all of those things and also encourage trade within the country and realize the possibilities of energy goods across the country, rather than tying ourselves more and more firmly into the United States, I would suggest we could reach full employment, balance the Budget, and pay off the national debt instead of adding to it every year as Conservatives have been forced to do too. They have added $100 billion over their three years, plus, in power. That is hardly something to be very proud of for people who are obsessed with the national debt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 hope the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) will stay around for a while, because we would like to explain some of the things he does not seem to have understood about public administration and the Government of this country.
Mr. Speaker, he started earlier by saying that it was a very thin Budget Speech, a Speech that lacked substance.
I can inform the Hon. Member that the Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on February 10, 1988, continued the policies in the first Budget brought down in early 1985.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Hon. Member would like to recall the circumstances in which Canadians, in 1984, decided to elect a Progressive Conservative Government.
I remember what the people in the riding of Portneuf wanted in 1984. And I also remember the election platform we presented to Canadians and especially to the people in the riding of Portneuf.
Mr. Speaker, we all remember that before 1984, interest rates were very high, and the annual inflation rate was around 12 per cent. We had incredible chronic unemployment. Young Canadians could not look forward to starting a family like their parents did, because there just weren't any jobs. More plants were closing than new ones starting up.
Meanwhile, we would regularly see Liberal and NDP Members attending grand openings of nature paths and small parks they were setting up all over the place, all because of these people who were being given jobs under federal programs, the so-called "twenty-week" programs dreamt up by the Liberal Government.
My father used to say that when he was a young lad, they had Valcartier's 20 cents. Some Members may recall Valcar-tier's 20 cents from the Depression. People were given 20 cents a day plus a package of tobacco and cigarette paper, and that is how they managed to survive.
The Liberals invented the 20-week job. Obviously, the people who worked at these jobs had a much better chance of doing so if they had the right connections.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, in 1984 Canadians were fed up with this approach. They asked the Conservatives to do what was necessary to put the economy back on its feet and create a situation in Canada where Canadians would be able to participate in the development of their country.
Mr. Speaker, that is what we did, that is what the Minister of Finance has done, that is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) did and that is what this Government has been able to do.
On February 10, the Minister of Finance may have brought down the least spectacular Budget this Parliament has seen in decades. We have not made any rash promises during the past four years, Mr. Speaker. Maybe not four, but almost four years. What we did was to put in place the mechanisms we promised, starting in September 1984.
Recently, I met people in my riding who asked me: "Mr. Ferland we have plans for a playground in our community. It would be good for the kids". I said: "Sure, but we don't have any money". They answered: "How come the federal Government doesn't have any money? You spend $100 billion annually. You must have $25,000 or $30,000 to help build a playground". But I said: "Let me tell you that our Government has reached the objective it set for itself in 1984, which was to revive the economy and renew the hopes and dreams of Canadians, something people had lost in 1984". So they said: "Now listen, we are developing this community and we need certain facilities". So 1 said: "Remember, in 1984 the Conservatives said: We have to make a choice between creating permanent jobs or building playgrounds. However, to create permanent jobs, first the economy has to be in good shape. To revive the economy, we have to deal with the deficit".
The former Minister of Finance, Mr. Lalonde, used to say that an annual deficit of $50 billion should be considered normal in Canada. I may remind you that the NDP never disagreed with this stand. In any case, you can put the Liberals and the New Democrats in a box, shake well, and one comes out green and the other comes out red. Philosophically, they are all the same.
So I told these people, Mr. Speaker: "We made a choice. We made cuts in the Government's discretionary spending, cuts totalling $4 billion the first year. The following year, in the second Budget, we cut $2 billion. Last year we cut $500 million. This year, we intend to cut $300 million in discretionary spending. Mr. Speaker, we have now cut a total of $6.8 billion in our Budgets, funds I am sure could have been used
February 23, 1988

to make our backbenchers, especially, look good in their ridings. Of course it is nice for a Member to be able to tell an association or a group in his community: "We are happy to give you this cheque to develop your project. It will help the community and put people to work for eight or ten weeks". However, that is not what we had in mind in 1984, as Members of this Government. In 1984. our objective was to create permanent jobs.
When we were elected, there was a whole series of job creation programs, a total of 24, Mr. Speaker. There were all kinds of programs, except programs that provided for permanent jobs. We did some housecleaning. We eliminated 18 programs and kept six. My constituents are particularly happy with one of those programs, the Job Development Program. This government took the initiative in working with the private sector, the municipalities as well as with non-profit-making organizations in order to create permanent jobs. And it has succeeded, Mr. Speaker. In my riding, hundreds of workers now have a permanent job thanks to this Canadian government program. And I can tell you that people thank me for that. Members do not get thanks very often, but when people have been unemployed for one or two years they do not mind thanking you for helping them find a job by creating a situation conducive to job creation.
Speaking of job creation, Mr. Speaker, before 1984 in my riding plants closing and job lay-offs were almost a regular occurence. But since 1984, Mr. Speaker, the trend was reversed. Although one may want to criticize the performance of the Conservative government, one cannot deny what has been achieved in my own riding and which is there for every one to see.
Since 1984, we have seen 36 expansion projects and the creation of new businesses with the assistance of the Federal Government. And in my riding it was the work of only one department, the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. The Opposition criticizes the work done by that Department but I can tell you that people in my riding are totally satisfied with the job done and they just want that Department to put even more money for development in my constituency. But from 1984 up to now the Federal Government has invested $4,056 million, thus allowing the private sector to carry out projects to the tune of $16,240,000. That is a lot of money, Mr. Speaker! Thirty-six businesses expanded or were established, and I don't mention those which did not need the help of the Government of Canada because they had enough financial backing to go at it alone, and also because as a result of the economic climate created by the Government throughout the country they could do it by themselves. They were proud to say that they did it all by themselves and they said so to the reporters. But what they don't forget to mention is the fact that if we are able today to invest without anybody's help, it is because of the policies implemented by the Conservative
The Budget-Mr. Ferland
Government. But this is another objective, Mr. Speaker, that the people from Portneuf in my riding has asked us to reach.
The people were asking me to put pressure on my Government, on the Ministers to get action along those lines.
I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Governmeent delivered the goods and that we can be proud as Canadians to have such a good Government, managed by men and women who took over an administration which was really terrible and transformed it into an administration worthy of a country like Canada.
Considering how the New Democrats and the Liberals behave in this House, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if they really want fairness in Canada. In 1984, indeed, we stated that we wanted fairness for each and all in this country. The most recent example that I believe Canadians will remember, particularly those from Quebec, and I know that residents of Portneuf are still reminding me about it, concerns Bill 22. Who filibustered Bill 22? That Bill was precisely about high technology, about our future, about research. Members from the NDP and the Liberal Party say that we do nothing for research. Yet, we introduced Bill 22. The New Democrats supported it, and even though they are against the Senate, they supported the Senate as well. That is something, Mr. Speaker! 1 say they are whited sepulchres. What else can I say? We cannot use other terms for fear of unparliamentary language. So I shall refrain. Nonetheless, it is outrageous. It is outrageous for Canadians and especially for Quebecers, for what were the New Democrats and Liberals doing by filibustering Bill C-22? They were doing, Mr. Speaker, what the Liberals had always been doing: They were creating a strong central Canada and weak eastern and western Canada and forcing East and West to go down on their knees to central Canada, that is southern Ontario.
And that is what they have done, Mr. Speaker, for where were the copying companies? They were in Ontario, not in Quebec. On the contrary, we had in Quebec innovative companies. Hundreds of millions of dollars were contributed by the private sector and were not coming out of the taxpayers pocket, Mr. Speaker. But no! The research must be done in Canada but not by the private sector. It must be done by the Government. They would have Canadians believe that people are not the Government. Well now, Mr. Speaker, when I travel through my riding I say to them: You are the Government. You are the people from whom we get the money. We get the money from your pockets, we do not ask for your permission, but we are the ones who decide how it is going to be spent. That is reality.
Provincial and municipal administrations do exactly the same thing. All Government levels in Canada do that, but indeed they have to provide sound financial management. If we were to listen to the socialists-small-s and capital-S, minor red or green socialists-we would take even more money out of their pockets to be able to make bigger deals and thus appear to be even more important. Budgets would be much

February 23, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Ferland
more impressive and the state would do even more. Still, Mr. Speaker, I am not convinced that the state managed by officials would do better with the money than the private sector or the individual who had to work to earn that money.
Why would these same individuals be against free trade? It just happened that way. I am sure the leader of the New Democratic Party does not come from Canada's most destitute region. I was told that the unemployment rate in his riding is something like 3 per cent. I certainly wish it was at that level in my riding, Mr. Speaker. In spite of the hundred of jobs which have been created, the unemployment rate there is still close to 12 per cent. "If it is good for Ontario", as the Portneuf people will say, "it is good for us too". The people in my riding are not afraid of the American market. We have papermills. We have sawmills and granite processing plants. We have cement plants. And do you know to whom our people are selling? To the Americans! And it is not in their mother tongue that they do! They have learned how to speak English and even American to be able to make themselves understood. They are not afraid of that. Quite the contrary, they are saying: "We are finally going to get the same opportunities as the people in Ontario". But we hear Premier Peterson of Ontario, supported by Mr. Broadbent, the NDP Leader, and Mr. Turner, the Liberal Leader, saying: "We are going to tear up this deal". Can you imagine that, Mr. Speaker? The Liberals and the NDPs are clearly demonstrating that they do not want to give a break to Canadians, whether they live in Western, Eastern or even Central Canada. That is unacceptable. It is as though the country had been governed for 75 years by a Liberal Government only for the benefit of Ontario. It is a fact that Quebec may have been slow understanding. It may have had to wait until the Conservative Party chose a leader from Quebec before it decided to trust him and elect him as Prime Minister in Ottawa with a Conservative Government. But I can tell you something, Mr. Speaker: Ever since a Conservative Government was elected in Ottawa, Quebec has had its fair share, as evidenced by ... Who are the staundest supporters of free trade, Mr. Speaker? The Governments of Quebec, Western Canada, and British Columbia. Why?
Because they are aware that their people will finally have an opportunity to make deals with the Americans, to expand and find new markets in the United States without having to go through Toronto, because we must admit, even if the NPDs and Liberals are loath to say so, that free trade has existed for twenty years in Ontario. It has clearly existed there for twenty years. So if it has been good enough for Ontario ... I remember the slogan: "If it is good for Ontario, it is good for Canada". But now, they have a new Premier... It was a Conservative Premier who was saying that then. Today, the Liberal Premier is saying the reverse: "If it is not good for Ontario, it is not good for Canada". It is funny! Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, if it is good for Canada, it must be good for Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia and New Brunswick. This is the case of the Free Trade Agreement. It is also the case of the Budgets introduced by Mr. Wilson in this House and of everything which the Governement of the Right Hon. Prime
Minister, Brian Mulroney, has accomplished in the last three and a half years. This is what we have tried to do, Mr. Speaker, and it is not always easy.
I was reading an article today by Rodrigue Tremblay. He is not just anybody; he is very well-known in Quebec. This is what he had to say: Without free trade, there would be only one major centre, Toronto. .. The reason is quite simple: The St. Lawrence valley is now attractive to investors, and the region of Montreal becomes an ideal location to gain access to all North America, especially to the Montreal/Boston-New York-Washington/Chicagop-Toronto triangle.
I know that my time is almost up, Mr. Speaker, but I want to say that everything the Government has done was done openly. The Government had said in 1984 that it would be difficult, but that it would be done. The Opposition says that we have increased taxes. However, not a single Quebecer, not a single Canadian, even if he only has a grade one education, knows that a Governement cannot work miracles and that, when there are debts, they have to be paid. Those debts were not created by the Conservative Party, but by the mismanagement of a Liberal Government in partnership with the New Democrats. Together, they brought Canada to the brink of bankruptcy. What we have done, Mr. Speaker, is to give back some hope to our youth, to all Canadians so that they may develop this country and put it back on track. We have given them proper direction and we shall continue to do so. After the next election, Mr. Speaker, you and I will still be here in this House to protect Canada's interests.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to be able to speak in the debate on the Budget recently presented to this House by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). It is a very curious document because it says so little. One wonders what could possibly have been in the mind of the Minister in bringing out such a bland document, a do-nothing Budget, a non-event, really. Is he saying there is nothing to be done, that the situation is rolling along beautifully? If so, nothing could be further from the truth.
We hear negative comments from all over the country. The business community says the deficit is too high. People from all walks of life say the Government is not concerned about their interests. Certainly if there is one group that must be listened to it is lower-income Canadians. This Budget, like previous Budgets, increases the disparities between the wealthy and not so wealthy. It is a sad commentary on our times that a country as wealthy as Canada should be neglecting people and areas of this country which need assistance in developing their economic possibilities.
Just look at the tone of this Budget, not only what is there but what is not; for example, the child care program. The Government told us it would be bringing forward a child care credit which would apply equally no matter the income of the person claiming the deduction. But it did not do that. It created a deduction of $4,000, which will of course be more significant to wealthy Canadians than it will be to lower-income Canadians. A person in a 29 per cent federal tax bracket will be able to save as much as $1,800 under that deduction, yet someone in a 17 per cent bracket will save only $1,000. That is not what we were led to believe the Government was going to do. We were told one thing and the Government did another.
It seems as though the Government always drifts away from ordinary Canadians when it brings down a Budget or makes its economic pronouncements. Not only does the Government seem to ignore low income Canadians and areas in which economic difficulties are prevalent, it seems to make matters worse. That is not right.
What did the Government do with this Budget? It increased excise taxes. Who will that hit? It will hit the Canadian motorist. The excise tax on gasoline will be increased significantly. Since the Government came to power it has imposed excise taxes on gasoline amounting to 5 cents per litre,

February 23, 1988
The Budget-Mr. MacLellan
inclusive of the tax that was imposed in this Budget. That 5 cents per litre is equivalent to 23 cents per gallon. This amount is higher than the amount of excise tax proposed by the former Minister of Finance, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), which he was planning to impose in his Budget in December of 1979. He wanted to impose an 18 cent per gallon excise tax. The Government has increased the sales tax. The sales tax also applies to gasoline. There will be a 1 cent per litre increase, which is incredible.
What does this mean? It means that the average Canadian family of two adults and two children will pay $1,200 more in taxes today than it was paying when the Conservative Government was elected in September, 1984. This is not getting to the problem of ordinary Canadians.
The speaker who spoke before me talked about the unemployment rate and how the Government wants to see equal opportunities throughout the country. That is not happening. There are not equal opportunities throughout the country. In fact the opportunities for certain Canadians are becoming fewer and fewer. The Member who spoke before me talked about the unemployment rate being 8.1 per cent nationally. In Nova Scotia it is 12.1 per cent. The Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) said that according to her own tabulations in her own constituency the unemployment rate there is 27 per cent. In my constituency on Cape Breton Island the unemployment rate is 21.1 per cent. It is higher by far than when the Government took office in 1984.
Yet what do we get from the Government? We get the general pronouncements with respect to its strong economic performance. This leads to the apology that perhaps this does not apply across the country, that there are certain areas the Government would like to see a little better off economically. That is all we get.
There is always an asterisk in the Budget about how it is too bad that certain areas of the country are not doing better economically, that certain people in certain areas are more prone to unemployment than people in more prosperous economic areas. That is just not good enough. The Government has been in power now for three and a half years. It is high time that something was done to correct the regional disparities, not making them worse than they were before.
We see continuing evidence that the Government does not care. It says that it will do something and immediately thereafter it says that it forgot all about it. It says these things for public consumption hoping that certain words, phrases or promises will stay in the minds of Canadians. Canadians might have been predisposed to think of these niceties when the Government was first elected, but they will no longer. They know that the words of the Government are hollow and that it does not mean anything that it says when it comes to helping low income Canadians and those living in areas of regional disparity.
What has the Government done? The Minister of Finance started off with his first statement which was not a Budget. It
was an economic statement that he put forward in November, 1984, in which he started to slash programs, including programs that were very necessary for Canadians.
One thing that bothered me in the energy field-something which bothered me then and continues to bother me now-is that the Government slashed programs which helped Canadians save on their energy expenses. Why would a Government do that? That certainly hits low income Canadians. The Government did away with those programs and said that they had never served their purpose. In effect, the Government said, "We are going to get away from actually throwing money at Canadians. We are going to promote programs but we are not going to give away money". It was right about one thing, it certainly did not give away any money. However, it has not been promoting programs either.
The difficulty is that those programs were important to Canadians. Conservation was the most successful aspect of the former Liberal Government's National Energy Program. That program saved Canada 75 million barrels of oil per year. That is something important to consider. It is important to take the strengths of a program or of a country and to build on them, not to destroy them. Destroying them not only does away with the program but hurts the people who the programs were intended to help. In most cases those people are low income Canadians. Not only does this affect the ability of people to pay for their energy, it also affects their ability to stay in their own homes. The conservation program was important in terms of allowing senior citizens and low income Canadians to remain in their own homes.
That was not the only program the Government destroyed. It reduced substantially the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan. It also cut back on RAP which was an important program giving assistance to Canadians who wanted to stay in their own homes. Not only is my constituency an area of high unemployment, it is an older area as well. It is important that people who are in their homes are able to fund repairs for their homes because if they cannot then they cannot stay in their homes. They will be condemned. What will happen then? They will find themselves without a place to live or the Government must provide public housing. Today, public housing costs between $40,000 and $50,000 per unit. Where is the advantage to Canadians? Where is the advantage to the Government?
The Government promised jobs. It has made many statements. Yet in the Budget the Government does not say what it promises to Canadians. It does not give an accounting of what it has said, showing us what has been delivered on. The Government ignores that. It ignores the promises it has made. It has gone on to make new promises. It wants to make further promises, which of course it has no intention of keeping.
It is important that Canadians know that the Government is not resolving their predicaments at all. What the Government is doing is trying to see what is its best position before going into another election. In the upcoming election Members of the
February 23, 1988

Government will run into a great number of skeptical Canadians. Canadians will no longer take the words of the Government at face value. They will not do that. They will be prepared to accept the promises of the Government, but they will be duly skeptical.

subsubtopic: RIGHTS OF UNBORN CHILDREN-CALL FOR INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we now have the intolerable situation that there is no federal law in place to protect in any way the rights of the unborn.
Because the right to life is obviously the supreme and highest of all human rights, the recent decision by the Supreme Court of Canada places an urgent requirement, not only on the Government which has the lead responsibility, but also on each and every parliamentarian to see to it that good legislation is passed.
As Members of Parliament we now have at last a rare opportunity, at the invitation of the Supreme Court, to pass legislation to protect the life and the rights of the unborn fetus. I want to make it clear again that I personally am opposed to abortion. But while it is obvious to me that the process of life starts at conception, I am sure that the courts will continue to argue over the legal definition as to when a human life begins, and our legislation will have to anticipate this problem.
However, I am deeply concerned that the Government may decide not to act, or that it may delay. Even if it does bring in legislation, there are dangerous signs that it will imitate a number of other countries, by only limiting protection of the fetus until after a fixed time such as 20 weeks following conception. Such legal rigidity would be tragic because it would deny the full protection of the law to the fetus at an earlier stage. We cannot afford to delay as we are talking about the survival of human life. I call upon the Government to give us an immediate commitment to a timeframe for action.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same subject which is an issue of urgent and pressing necessity. Since the recent Supreme Court decision striking down the abortion law, Canada has become the only civilized nation in the world which has no legislation protecting the unborn child.
Yet a recent Gallup poll of Canadians revealed that 53 per cent of Canadians want some legislation to protect the fetus. They are looking to the federal Government for leadership on this emotional issue.
I recognize and support the current Government on the process of consultation with the provinces prior to the introduction of legislation. Let us move with speed and deliberation. Let us take the lead and demonstrate to Canadians and to the world that we, as a nation, have the courage to balance the rights of women with the protection of human life. No group has unlimited rights.
Every civilized nation will ultimately be measured by how it treats it most vulnerable, those who cannot speak for themselves and who ask for nothing but a chance. I urge the Government to act with courage and compassion.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise today to insist on the resignation of the Minister responsible for aboriginal affairs. The Minister has broken the trust relationship with Canada's first citizens.
The 1973 ruling of the Supreme Court of Canada on the Nishga case brought Canada into negotiations on the comprehensive claim to the Nass Valley. The Minister has now crushed those negotiations and refuses to act in good faith.
Since 1940 the Lubicon Band has sought the respect and assistance of the federal Crown for the historic lands of the Lubicon people. The Minister has chosen to fund the Dai-shawa Corporation to log the very lands that the Lubicon seek, in contravention of Cabinet requirements for an impact evaluation. This is bad faith.
Since 1985 the Lytton and Mount Currie Bands have sought to meet with the Minister for assistance in preparing their case on the Stein Valley. Even today they are here in Ottawa and the Minister has refused to see them. This is bad faith.
The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of British Columbia has encouraged aboriginal people in British Columbia to stand up for their rights. The first citizens of Canada cannot put

February 23, 1988
trust in a Minister who will not meet and who will not negotiate. Race relations are disintegrating in British Columbia as a result of the calculated budget cuts combined with accelerated pressure on the lands and resources.
The Minister must resign because these federal policies are forcing natives and non-natives into confrontation and, potentially, violence.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week is National Boy Scout and Girl Guide Week. I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate all the boy scouts and the girl guides in the federal riding of York South- Weston.
On February 12 the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) and I had the pleasure of attending the First Weston
Beaver-Cub and Scouts fund raising dance. We were extremely honoured that evening to have been made honorary scouts of Weston. Scout Leader, Mr. Kevin Breakey, administered our oath and gave us our scout scarves, which I am wearing here today in the House. I promised the boys that I would wear this scarf in the House today.

Jeanne Sauve.

Incidentally, 15 per cent of all funds raised on this particular project go to youth education in Third World countries.
The scouting oath is based on the following principles:
I promise to serve my God, my Queen, my country and my fellow man and
to be wise in the use of my resources.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF LIBERAL PARTY
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF LIBERAL PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me to pose a question. When would a free trade agreement no longer be a free trade agreement? Doubtless, Mr. Speaker, your impeccable logic would conclude that if it were torn up it would no longer be a free trade agreement.
But, Mr. Speaker, Liberal utterings indicate a greater freedom in labile Liberal logic than that available to the rest of us, because there are Liberal voices who suggest that we are wrong. Perhaps we did not have the question right. Perhaps our question should have been, when is a commitment to tear up a free trade agreement no longer a commitment to tear up a free trade agreement? Perhaps the answer is when Liberal corporate donors say that such a commitment is to commit suicide. A conundrum to find an answer to which the Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) and the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) were dispatched to Washington, to find a new commitment perhaps to avoid committing financial suicide.

Mr. Speaker, the year 1988 is special to Ukrainian Canadians as it marks the millennium of Christianity in Ukraine. It also reminds us that, although the Soviet Government has claimed to have adopted a spirit of openness or "glasnost", persecution of Ukrainian Orthodox and Ukrainian Catholic clergy continues. As well, the Soviet Government has perpetrated numerous human rights violations, disregarding the statutes of the Helsinki Accord, to which it is a signatory.
An example is the case of Yuri Shukhevych who has been in prison for 36 of the last 40 years simply because he is the son of General Roman Shukhevych, the Commander in Chief of the Ukrainian insurgent army who was killed in 1950. Today Yuri Shukhevych remains in prison in very poor health.
Yuri Shukhevych's "guilt" lies not in commission, but in association. This is a travesty of human rights. Until the Soviet Government ceases human rights violations there can be no glasnost and no justice.
Lest we misinterpret the true intentions of the Soviet Government, I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Government of Canada to pressure the Soviet Government for the release of Yuri Shukhevych and other prisoners of conscience in the Soviet Union.
We all want peace, but not without freedom.

HAMILTON AIRPORT-TEST FLIGHTS-EFFECT ON RESIDENTS' SLEEP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at almost exactly this hour in Hamilton City Hail, regional councillor Ann Sloat is delivering the same message to concerned residents of Ancaster as I am telling Hon. Members in this House.
The entire Hamilton-Wentworth area desires to get as much air traffic as possible into Hamilton Airport. The just announced Pan Am express service from Hamilton to New York is great.
What we do not need, as just one example of sleep disturbing activity, is a major airline which purchases giant airbuses from France and then test flies them, with 36 take-offs and landings from one o'clock to three o'clock in the morning.

maintopic: MERGER AND SALE OF ELDORADO NUCLEAR AND SASKATCHEWAN MINING DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION
MERGER AND SALE OF ELDORADO NUCLEAR AND SASKATCHEWAN MINING DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our billion dollar Minister of State for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs (Mrs. McDougall) has struck again. Perhaps the most disturbing part of the Minister's press conference yesterday in Saskatoon was her statement that the proceeds of the sale of a merged Eldorado Nuclear and Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation would go toward retiring the debt of the two companies.
What this means is that the people of Canada will be forced to assume $600 million in debt, and the people of Saskatchewan another $450 million, for a total of over $1 billion. The only people who will benefit will be those able to buy shares, not the ordinary citizens of Canada who advanced the hundreds of millions of dollars necessary to establish both these public enterprises.
Since both Eldorado and Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation have been presented to the public as viable, well managed companies, why do the purchasers need an additional public subsidy of $1 billion in order to be persuaded to buy?
Clearly the Government wants future high share prices and increased profits for its private sector friends. Under this proposal future profits will be paid for, in advance, by the Canadian public, thanks to the Conservative Government.

speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Jean Sirois, friend of the Prime Minister, has caused untold grief as Chairman of Telefilm. Yesterday the Minister was too clever by half. subsubtopic: RESIGNATION OF FORMER EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I tabled the official, signed letter that Mr. Pearson sent to me. I admit, of course, that there was a second letter. I may also say to the Hon. Member that the action I took on the difficulties in Telefilm would have been the same regardless of what letter I had received because we knew that Telefilm was in financial difficulty. We knew that there had been difficulties with management, and we moved immediately to ensure that there was an audit made of the finances of Telefilm, and that financial systems and a financial management team were put in place.
It is interesting to note that the film industry itself, the association representing some 200 film producers in this country, wrote to me and said: "We share your distress over
recent attempts to make political mileage out of, what for us, was old news. We have been working with Jean Sirois in trying to get everything ready for a new Executive Director".

The executive director reported that Telefilm was overcommitted to the tune
of $48 million.
Would she be prepared to correct her misinformation and acknowledge that it was Chairman Sirois on October 26 who made that unfounded announcement?

Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that we had been advised by the former Executive Director that there was probably going to be a lapse of $53 million. Then through the month of September we learned that that was not so. subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER MEET INDIAN CHIEFS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat surprised by the prefatory nature of the comments of my hon. friend with regard to our commitment to aboriginal rights.
I had the privilege of chairing two First Ministers, conferences in Canada, seeking justice for our aboriginal people and seeking the appropriate constitutional amendment that would deliver that justice. We came extremely close to securing an historic agreement. We have to try again.
If I may say so, I, along with many others, was instrumental in working out an agreement that I believe was satisfactory to the native people and all the environmental groups with regard to South Moresby in British Columbia. That was a landmark settlement which very much favoured the aboriginal presence and economic development in British Columbia. We have introduced a number of comprehensive initiatives.
It is with a great deal of pleasure that I regularly meet with aboriginal leaders here and across the country. I have done so from the day I was sworn in and will continue to do so on a regular, ongoing basis. Any time that it is in any way productive, I will be happy to do so.

speechtext:
Order, please. The Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLel-lan) has seven minutes left for debate plus 10 minutes of questions and comments. Before he commences, may I say that I hope Hon. Members will continue their conversations behind the curtain.
The Budget-Mr. MacLellan

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I was interrupted for Question Period I was discussing the inadequacies of the Budget brought down by the Government, particularly with respect to the areas of this country which are undergoing economic difficulty, to those who are without jobs, and to a lot of those who are employed but who are not getting support from the Government in obtaining the type of job security they should have. I am pleased that the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret) is here because a lot of this relates to his Department and the difficulty people have had in trying to follow through on what the Government has said it is going to do.
To give an example, we have the recent closure of the coke ovens at the Sydney Steel Corporation. This closure was of course directly related to the strike because they were not due to close until June. There are now another 125 men out of work in an area where the unemployment rate is 21.1 per cent, according to Statistics Canada, but where the actual rate is considerably higher.
Ten years ago those men said they wanted some kind of pension security because the coke ovens, then owned by the Cape Breton Development Corporation, were sold to the Sydney Steel Corporation. They went from a federal Crown corporation to a provincial Crown corporation. When these men, who had been at DEVCO for about 20 years, went with Sysco, they expected their pension benefits would go with them. Yet they now find that that is not the case. Men who worked for DEVCO for 35 or 40 years now have about 15 years seniority so far as pension benefits are concerned, mainly because the federal Government failed to honour its commitment to those men. This is treachery of the highest order. It is not against the law but it certainly goes against the grain and the stomachs of the Canadian public. It cannot be allowed to continue.
Of course, the country will rectify this in the next federal election but until then, the Government, particularly the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, should look into it once again. The steel workers have written to him about it and have not received an answer. I think the Minister should at least give them an answer on this very important question. These men remained in the same jobs, it was simply that the ownership of the ovens changed hands. Yet now they do not have seniority or their pension benefits. All they have is perhaps vacation rights.
Tom Kent, when he was President of the Cape Breton Development Corporation, promised those workers they would have their pension benefits and seniority, but that promise has not been kept. Therefore, I ask the Minister if he would be so kind as to look into this matter. As he can appreciate, it is a major concern in a very difficult time at the Sydney Steel Corporation. I hope also that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) would look into the promises and statements he has made with respect to the commitment to cleaning the tar ponds and Muggah Creek in Sydney. The commitments

February 23, 1988
The Budget-Mr. MacLellan
that were made by the Minister of the Environment have not been kept.
Fie also referred to the workers at the coke ovens. He said that when the coke ovens would be closed, which was supposed to be in June, there would be various benefits given to these workers, including job retraining. Unfortunately, because of the strike the closing was moved up to a couple of weeks ago. Yet we have heard absolutely nothing about this job retraining. These are things that should be remembered by the Government. These are initiatives which should be included in the Budget, not only because they are important in economically disadvantaged areas but because they are initiatives that have already been talked about and, in many cases, promised.
I ask that the Government look at the question of regional disparity to ensure that the people are not misled and that there are programs. I ask the Government to do this so that people will not be wasted. There are areas of the country in which there are shortages of manpower. Yet we have people who are not being utilized to their maximum benefit. That is a crime. A person only has one life. It is paramount that the Government do what it can to make the life of each individual as meaningful as possible. That is something that the Government should keep in mind. A great part of this meaningfulness has to do with a career that a person has which is not only for his or her benefit but for the benefit of their families as well.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the Hon. Member very closely. Will he share with the House any good news that he has about Cape Breton? We have heard many negative comments and yet only today I received three letters from different people on the Island, all of whom wrote about how encouraged they are because new industries are opening. The writers of these letters have pointed out that for the first time some people are showing a new confidence in that the Island is bettering its position. In short, many more people are now working.
Since the Hon. Member is from the area, will he share any thoughts on this issue? Is there not some good news from Cape Breton?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is of course good news, as the Hon. Member has said. In particular I would like to mention the tax credit that was implemented when the Hon. Member was the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion which has gone a long way to encourage new industry to come to Cape Breton. There have been some benefits derived from that tax credit. Industries have located on the Island, particularly on the north side.
As the Hon. Member will appreciate, these industries require a lengthy lead time in order to set up to begin operations. In a great many cases we are not looking for large industries. We are looking for industries with 90 or 100 jobs. They are good industries. The problem is that while we have some new industries which, hopefully, will play an important
part in the economic future of industrial Cape Breton, we are now at the point of losing jobs faster than we are gaining them.
What is happening? There will be about 35 new jobs at Magna, which will be followed by another couple of hundred new jobs in the next year, we hope. Last week the management of National Sea Products stated that it is reducing its work force at its plant in North Sydney by 100. Some 125 jobs were lost at the coke ovens just two weeks ago. A couple of years ago some 600 jobs were lost at the heavy water plant. A few hundred jobs were lost at the Cape Breton Development Corporation. The Sydney Steel Corporation, which employed 3,600 people about 10 years ago, now employs 1,200, minus the 125 jobs at the coke ovens. What I understand is that both the provincial and the federal level of Governments will mothball the blast furnace. Thus an industry that once employed 3,600 people will be diminished to 600. That is a drastic reduction in employment. The new industries coming in will not be able to replace the jobs that we have lost and are losing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Hon. Member acknowledges that the tax credits have been beneficial as far as the area is concerned. I suggest that some of the grant programs have also helped. I suggest that the guarantee that will be put in place under the Atlantic opportunities approach will help as far as borrowing is concerned, particularly the interest buy-downs.
The Hon. Member has thrown out certain figures with respect to rising unemployment. While I think that each Member of the House has great concern for the type of hardship that has been suffered over the years by the people of Cape Breton, in fairness the Hon. Member should acknowledge that Statistics Canada has shown that something over
2,000	direct jobs have been created in the last three years in Cape Breton. Directly and indirectly some 9,000 jobs have been created also. When we cite certain reductions we must also weigh the positive aspects, something that I think is encouraging. I hope that it will continue. Will the Hon. Member confirm what I have been saying?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot confirm what the Hon. Member has said. There have been jobs brought forward as a result of incentives and through other business practices. I would not say that they have been in the order of 2,000 jobs.
Another concern I have is that a great many of the jobs that have been created in industrial Cape Breton and other areas are not full-time jobs. For instance, full-time jobs with benefits at Sysco, the Cape Breton Development Corporation, the heavy water plants, the fish processing plants and smaller industries are diminishing. Many jobs that have been created are part-time jobs in fast food industries and department stores that do not have any benefits whatsoever. These are not jobs in which people can face the future. While it is important to have them and while it is much better than not having any work at all, it still does not give any kind of structure to developing an economic base in an area such as Cape Breton.
February 23, 1988

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed an honour for me to enter into the budget debate and to respond to some of the views expressed by Members on this side of the House as well as by Members opposite. 1 was glad to hear some of the comments made by members of the Opposition. They give us some indication as to the way that they see Canada and the way in which they intend to campaign for the upcoming federal election. It lets us see how they intend to make Canada a better nation, to use some of their words.
They seem to criticize the way in which Canada is going. In the next few minutes I intend to discredit their assertions that the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has not done a good job. I can prove that he has done a very good job. I hope to do that in short order. First, I would like to refer to the Budget Speech. I will not repeat many of the things stated by the Finance Minister, but I think that he made some statements that nobody in this House can dispute.
He indicated that this country has become number one in economic growth since 1984. That is compared to the other western nations, the Group of Seven. In the past three years the Finance Minister's Budgets have had a tremendous impact on in bringing Canada into that position. Members of the opposition do not like to admit it, but they cannot deny that all indications are that that in fact has happened.
Members of the opposition Parties do not stand up and mention much about job creation. They pick a little corner here or there, but they do not talk too much about the fact that the unemployment rate has dropped since 1984 over-all, nation-wide, by some 3.5 percentage points. The opposition Parties do not want to admit that that is an improvement, and one has to wonder why. The Minister of Finance referred to
1.1	million jobs more now than there were in 1984. With some kind of mathematical genius the opposition Members state that that does not mean anything, that it has no bearing. The opposition Members and the people who support that position should look at their neighbours who are working now who were not working before. They must have great difficulty, Mr. Speaker.
Let us talk about interest rates. I recall, and so will Members who were in the House then, the early 1980s and those devastating interest rates under a Liberal regime. The reduction of interest rates has encouraged savings on a $50,000 mortgage of $1,200 per year. That is a direct benefit to Canadians. There is now a realization of that fact by the New Democratic Party. Members of that Party are now standing up and making the statement that the interest rate should be reduced by one percentage point, and that will be their
The Budget-Mr. Holtmann
platform. During the next election I can guarantee that the New Democrats will walk around this country and state, "If we get elected, we will reduce the interest rates one percentage point". What they fail to understand is that the Government has already reduced it by approximately four percentage points. In fact, that has stabilized and a whole new economy is shaping up.
In his Budget Speech, the Minister stated that "business is confident. The pace of investment has increased sharply". We do not hear the Opposition on that point. He states that "consumers are confident". 1 think that that is very evident.
I wish to indicate the importance of the private sector. The Minister made a few statements in that regard. He stated that "the driving force behind productivity, growth and job creation is a dynamic private sector". Finally, more and more we have got Government out of business and we see the private sector handling it far more efficiently and effectively.
Even the New Democratic Party of Manitoba is getting out of some public corporations because it does not know how to run them. I hope that the Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) hears this and hears it well. The New Democrats in Manitoba have a goose of a time running some public corporations and want to sell them. Why? Because Governments cannot do it as effectively as private business.
The Minister went on to state, "To encourage this dynamism the Government has taken far reaching measures to modernize the regulatory environment for business, reform the federal tax system, and secure markets for our exports". The Minister mentioned expanding trade. Some Members talked in a ridiculous fashion about ripping up the free trade agreement. Since then we have heard that even our trading neighbours to the south who have some difficulties with it are sure that the opposition Members, should they ever come to power, would not rip it up. One other area in the debate that I would like to enter into, and I heard some comments on it this morning, is that the Minister introduced a one cent a litre tax on gasoline. We heard doom and gloom about that increase of one cent per litre. Canadians will recall the many programs that this Government introduced that the opposition Parties condemned because the Government was not spending enough of the taxpayers' money. When the Minister had to raise a little revenue by adding one cent a litre to gasoline, the opposition Parties condemned that and stated, "How could people afford it?" I did a little calculation. If the average person was driving a medium-sized car and burned one tank of gas a month, some might burn more, some might burn less, that is about 50 or 60 litres. That is 50 or 60 cents a week. That adds up to perhaps $30 a year of additional revenue from Canadians, which is

certainly not a tax grab. I wanted to point out those few facts when I referred to the Budget of the Minister of Finance.

Our study finds that there have been significant improvements made in financial controls. The government now has systems and procedures that provide essential financial controls. Departments have corrected the fundamental weaknesses identified in the 1970s.
Do the Members here remember the 1970s? I am sure that they do.

Are you listening out there? A decade ago the Auditor General could not give any Canadian assurance of the recklessness with which the former Liberal administration spent its money. It is plain. It is in black and white, and he now has a better feeling. "Today I can do so", he goes on to say, "the essential framework is in place. There is one man in the House of Commons, the Hon. Minister of Finance who brought that back under control. I think he deserves a lot of credit for doing just that.

As a matter of fact, just yesterday the Hon. Member for Regina West an honourable member of the New Democratic Party, had something to say about the Budget. I think Canadians want to know just where the New Democratic Party stands, and I think this long-term Member has expressed it in a way that would shock everybody. We have always operated on the basis that every Government goes into debt most of the time,-
Can people imagine that a Government should automatically operate on the premise that it is going to be in debt, in the hole, broke? Is that what is their desire? -we still say-that a nation has different kinds of debts. There is constructive debt-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, almost a year ago, on March 16, 1987, speaking in the House, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made the following statement:
We are in the process of building two Canadas, one which is rich and
promising and one which is underdeveloped and underemployed.
The Budget we are debating today simply accelerates the process described by the Prime Minister, the process of making disparities between the rich and the poor even more apparent.
Let me, for the benefit of the Hon. Member for Selkirk- Interlake (Mr. Holtmann), put on the record some of the results of Tory Budgets. An average family of four earning $35,000 per year annually will pay $1,000 more in taxes this year than it did in the year the Conservatives took power. Until this Budget, that amount was $1,400 per family, but the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), realizing that we are coming closer and closer to an election, has in this Budget

February 23, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
given back $400 of the $1,400 in taxes he had imposed on ordinary families until this year.
The only people in Canada who will benefit from this Budget, the only people who will pay less tax than they have paid until now, are the very few wealthy people at the top. According to the Government's own estimates, fully one-quarter of non-taxpayers, almost 9,000 in the last year for which we have records, will still go untaxed. Over 250 Canadians who had incomes of more than $200,000 and who paid no income tax in the last year for which we have records will continue to be able to pay no income tax.
At the same time as we sock it to ordinary Canadians and give tax cuts to the wealthy, the same situation is occurring in respect to Canada's largest, wealthiest corporations. In 1986, Alcan Aluminum made $220 million in profits and paid no tax at all. In fact, it got a tax credit. In 1986, Xerox Canada made a profit of $115 million and got a tax credit of over $10 million. In 1986, Union Carbide of Canada made a profit of $28 million and paid no taxes. In 1987, Bramalea Consolidated made $51 million in profits and paid no taxes at all.
I want to talk about some of the problems which this Budget ignores completely. First I would like to quote from the preamble of the 1966 Canada Assistance Plan legislation, legislation which was endorsed by all Members of Parliament from all political Parties which were represented in the House at the time. The preamble reads:
-the provision of ADEQUATE assistance to and in respect of persons in
need and the prevention and removal of the causes of poverty and dependence
on public assistance ARE THE CONCERNS OF ALL CANADIANS-
The Canadian Council on Social Development points out in its analysis of the budget proposal brought forward which we are now debating that there is no provision in the Budget for increasing help to Canadian families living below the poverty line although the number of such people is now 851,000, up from 745,000 in 1980. That is the situation.
If one spends a little time in any city in Canada, from Newfoundland on the East Coast to Vancouver Island on the West Coast, one sees that the number of people who are so needy and desperate for help, the number of people who appear regularly at food banks operated by churches, native organizations and community organizations, is increasing rapidly from week to week. The number of charitable organizations which are handing out used clothing is increasing very rapidly. We are going back to the situation in the 1930s which most Canadians thought we would never experience again. Tens of thousands of people are having to depend on charity to meet their basic needs.
We have asked the Government to deal with that. We have asked the Government to meet with the provincial Ministers who deal with welfare and, if necessary, make studies which will indicate very clearly that the level of assistance paid to
people in need is far below that which is needed for them to live with some dignity and in some comfort.
I have done this in Winnipeg. I know of the work which is being done by organizations such as the Stella Mission, Rossbrook House, the Salvation Army, and many other organizations. They tell anyone who talks to them that they do this because there is a need. Without exception, people throughout the country who are involved in such charitable works agree that they are doing this because the need is there, but they think it is a disgrace that in a country as wealthy as Canada charity is needed on an increasing scale.
None of these problems have been dealt with by the Government. The economies in most western industrialized countries have improved and unemployment in Canada is down, as it is in the United States. However, except for the unemployment levels in Ontario and parts of Quebec, unemployment levels throughout the country are as high now as they were when the Government took office.
It is not only the poorly educated and the illiterate who are unemployed. Skilled workers and people who had highly paid jobs in financial institutions are now unemployed. In eight of the ten provinces unemployment is still high and indeed in parts of the two provinces in which employment has grown the fastest there are still crisis situations. Northern Ontario and most of the Province of Quebec east of Montreal still have unemployment rates which are completely unacceptable.
What has the Government done about this? It has failed to ensure that our social programs keep pace in terms of increased funding with the rate of inflation.
The federal Government has refused to deal realistically with the federal minimum wage which has been frozen for some years at $4 an hour. That rate is the second lowest in Canada while it was once almost the highest. People who work for $4 an hour, even if they work full time, still live in poverty. The Government, which has been so generous to our major corporations and to a very small number of very wealthy Canadians whose incomes are very high, has partially deindex-ed many of the social programs which were built over almost 50 years. The Government has partially deindexed the family allowance, the child tax credit, and the income tax brackets.
The Government is happy to do this because it really believes that the state should do less for the people of Canada rather than more.
To certain people on the right, and that includes almost all the Conservative Members of Parliament, cut-backs in social services are necessary to diminish the expectation of ordinary people of what government should do. The Government wants to keep working people docile for whatever jobs and working conditions are provided. We have, therefore, seen a tremendous increase in the number of people who work part time. When you work part time, of course, you do not get benefits such as holiday pay, unemployment insurance, and pensions,
February 23, 1988

which full-time permanent employees have come to expect to receive in their total wage packet for the work which they do.
We believe that one of the greatest challenges for our Party is to reverse these policies of neglect and uncaring and restate the purpose of our society so that all Canadians can legitimately expect to have jobs, adequate housing, and an education which will permit them to meet their needs and the needs of the country throughout the rest of the 1980s and the 1990s. There is nothing in this Budget which gives us any assurance that these objectives will be met.
I want to deal specifically with one of the major failures of the Government. In	the	first Throne Speech brought forwardby the Government	in	1984	there was a	promise that theGovernment would	make a	major effort	to deal with thedisastrous situation	of	fully	20 per cent	of the people of
Canada being functionally illiterate. Hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are in the labour force or will be entering the labour force in the next few years do not have the education, knowledge, or ability to fill the jobs which are and will be available. These jobs will require a great deal more education than was required years ago because of the tremendous changes in technology which require a much more well educated workforce than we have had.
Numberless studies have been done about the situation of the tremendous number of Canadians who are functionally illiterate. To those studies we can now add a study commissioned by a business task force on literacy which operates out of the City of Toronto and which tabled a report several weeks ago which confirmed the finding of earlier studies that a fifth of Canadians are functionally illiterate. According to them, it is costing $10.7 billion a year to permit this terrible situation to continue. In fact, they calculate that of that $10.7 billion, $4.2 billion is the cost to business through industrial accidents, lost productivity and training expenses.
The Government promised in its Speech from the Throne after it was elected that it would take major steps to deal with this problem. A few months ago, at the National Conference on Scientific Research and Technology in Toronto, the Prime Minister reaffirmed that pledge. The Secretary of State has made similar statements.
However, when we look at the record we see that the Government has only given us more talk and no action. There are groups in every province in Canada working with people who are functionally illiterate. To a large extent, these are people who grew up in rural areas, native people and new immigrants. While they are attempting to help tens of thousands of these functionally illiterate people, the fact is that there are five million people in Canada who are functionally illiterate. There will be terrible consequences for this country in the near future if that situation is permitted to continue.
Canada is entering an era when the number of people entering the labour force will decline each year, yet there will
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
be difficulty filling those jobs due to the increasing number of functionally illiterate people. All we have from the Secretary of State is talk and good will, but no money.
The record of the Department of Employment and Immigration, which was poor under the Liberals and is poor under the Conservative Government, is even worse. The Department has spent only a very small percentage of its total expenditures to train illiterate people simply because such a program does not bring quick results in terms of job creation. Instead, it has taken the easy route by training those already literate to become welders, machinists or computer operators because such jobs will be available soon after training is completed.
The Department has not faced up to the fact that if it does not help people overcome their illiteracy, it is condemning those people to live on welfare, unemployment insurance or accept the poorest, lowest paid jobs available. The then Liberal Government should be condemned for such an approach, and the Conservative Government should be condemned for continuing that policy. There is a major crisis on our hands in this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Mr. Speaker, does my colleague believe that the Government knows the meaning of disparity in this country? Hon. Members on that side of the House brag about the reduction of unemployment. However, we know that economic cycles come and go.
When we are talking about regional disparity in Canada, we are talking about the difference in the national rate compared to the provincial rate. For example, in 1949, before Confederation, Newfoundlanders earned, per capita, almost 49 per cent of the average Canadian income. Last year it was 55 per cent, so that we have seen a narrowing of the disparity by 6.7 per cent in 38 years.
At that rate, it will be another 250 years before Newfoundlanders earn the same per capita income as the national average. That is what we mean by disparity.
The gap in the unemployment rate in Newfoundland compared to that in Canada is very large. Will the Member comment on the fact that the attempt to narrow the disparity in this area has not been successful? Does this Budget make any real commitment to change that?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most Canadians know about the disparities. Most Canadians know that in eight of the ten provinces the rate of unemployment is just as high as it was when the Government took office.
The Member for Selkirk-Interlake was proud of the reduction in the rate of unemployment. Of course we agree, but Conservatives do not admit that there are still over one

February 23, 1988
Adjournment Motion
million unemployed. There are many areas in this country where people still live in poverty. A good example is Selkirk- Interlake represented by that Conservative Member who is so proud of the Government. Fie criticized government deficits. If we have to keep the deficit down, there will be no money for the native communities in his constituency who live in such deplorable housing.
We have to face up to the tremendous disparities in incomes and services between wealthy parts of Canada such as southern Ontario, and the rural or isolated areas where there is not only a tremendously high rate of unemployment but where services, whether it be education, health or anything else, are still deplorable and disgraceful.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in my hon. colleague's comments, particularly with respect to the question of illiteracy. I know he is very concerned about those who have been unemployed because of this handicap. I wonder if he has any comments to make with respect to prevention.
I know that when the Special Committee on Child Care toured the country we heard over and over again that there are ways, involving a relatively small investment and by starting with children at the pre-school level, of preventing much of the dysfunctioning which occurs later in life. I am thinking particularly of the Head Start program which has been very successful in the U.S. Research has shown that children from disadvantaged homes, where perhaps their parents were illiterate, were helped to function much better and make much better use of school after having been involved in these enrichment programs. As a result, when they got to be teenagers there was a much lower rate of adolescent problems. They stayed in school longer, there were not as many teenage pregnancies or drug abuse. It seems to me that is an area of great importance and it would require an investment of only a small amount of money. Yet the Government seems to be looking for every means possible to delay in getting on with the child care program which should include enriched programs of this kind.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is no question that some other countries, such as the U.S. with its Head Start program, and Sweden, Denmark and West Germany, have had a great deal of success in overcoming problems such as illiteracy with programs designed specifically to help people in difficulty. I agree completely with the Hon. Member that one of the best things we could do would be to improve our child care system. We should have a day care system which would not only help young children begin to learn to read and write, but which would permit their parents, particularly in the single-parent families, to work or improve their education, or get training in fields with employment prospects. Of course, all these things can be and should be done but we have a Government intent on reducing the deficit and it is just not prepared to move on any of these ideas.
